Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Is there a concept in math or science you once understood for an instant, but then lost your grasp on the concept?
Answer: Yes; this happens to me all the time. To really understand a concept, I have to keep studying it, slowly getting to know it by creating a mental image of it and creating the associations and intuitions that tie it to other concepts and intuitions that I already have. That happens gradually and with stops and starts and breakthroughs to insight: those Aha! moments. But, as with so much learning, it’s use it or lose it. Mental images fade, even when the intuitions remain. Sometimes, it feels almost as if I’ve lost more understanding than I’ve ever gained. One episode, several years ago, really highlighted how much you (well, I) can forget, and it always makes me laugh to think about: I was browsing some past research papers when I discovered this beautifully written paper full of really elegant and relevant research, just the sort of results that I could use for my own work and just the sort of mathematical style that I like. Excited and intrigued, I flicked to the title page to read who the author of this excellent paper was. The author was me.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Was it easier to do research in the past when so many things were unexplored and unsaturated?
Answer: Thanks for a very interesting question! Looking back at the sciences of past ages, we might find a certain smug and condescending pleasure to see that we understand much more now than people did then. And, conversely, we might find ourselves a little jealous that a few of those people had access to so many low-hanging fruits of knowledge. You might even have day-dreamed, like me, of traveling back in time to cash in on your superior knowledge and insights. That’s all natural to think and feel - but it is also naive and arrogant. As the speculative fiction Doomsday Book by Connie Willis very nicely illustrates, our present knowledge is often useless and incompatible in past contexts, just like past knowledges are useless and incompatible in our present contexts. We have so much knowledge and insight-generating capacities today but they relate to the way in which we see the world today. In the past, people were interested in other things than we are today, and so much past valuable knowledge has been lost, partly because it is no longer needed. But my comments above only set the setting for the question at hand. To be sure, people were interested in other things then than we are today, but was it easier then to explore and to conduct research in ways that were meaningful back then? I would say, on the whole: No. Yes, so much knowledge was there to be discovered, and, from our point of view, was easy to discover. However, their questions were different, and their understanding was too. If you were to discover quantum mechanics four hundred years ago, then how would you even begin to express your ideas to anyone without sounding like a madman? And even if you were accepted and applauded as a respectable researcher, how would anyone understand your ideas? Boole’s monograph The Laws of Thought from 1854 was respectedly overlooked until nearly a century later, when its abstruse equations were discovered to exactly what was needed to create the DNA of our modern computers. Leibniz’ more abstract ideas smell of visionary insight that we are not ready to be able to understand and use, even now four centuries later. More prosaically, we should also be fair and take into account practical circumstances. Despite our presently alarming rates of illiteracy and innumeracy, we are on the whole unimaginably better educated in academic ways than our foreparents (and unimaginably less educated in non-academic ways). There were far fewer people back then, and far fewer of those people to be lucky enough to get education, and far fewer of those educated to be lucky enough to gain employment through research, than now. You might find yourself among the lucky very few to find a position in some college or academy, or as royal trophy-mathematician, akin to magician, but your duties would include a large teaching or administration load. You would have colleagues but not the wide and lightning-quick network of colleagues and knowledge databases of today. You would essentially have to pioneer your fields of research and invent the language in which to express it. So, yes, it was easier, back then, to find the sort of knowledge that we value today. But they didn’t look for and appreciate that sort of knowledge as much back then, and there were fewer to find it. For those few, it was not easier to find that knowledge than we would find it to be, given circumstances. The famous explorers and scientists of old are famous for a reason: their findings are important but, more importantly, we celebrate their considerable efforts to find their findings.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: If the afterlife was proved irrefutably by science, how would this affect you?
Answer: As a curious person, that would excite me tremendously. It would validate the otherwise nearly meaningless notion of “me-ness”; that in itself I could spend the rest of my life trying to make sense of. Which entities cross from this life to other lives? Plants? Ecosystems? Patterns? Is this a linear progression of Lives, or are there more dimensions of progression, or perhaps something non-linear? Do these determine each other, like LEGO bricks falling on top of each other in a chaotic heaps, or do they overlap and flicker in and out, fractionally and putatively, like quantum froth? Does it get even weirder than this? My guess is: Yes, almost certainly. But, also: me-ness is nearly illusory, and will flicker out way before my overall body does. To more scientific-minded people, the obvious questions would be: what and how is the Afterlife, and how does it relate to this life. Were there Before-lives, and how many? Is there a pattern here? Can we weigh and even compare Lives? Is there a Best or a Worst Life? Can we draw some graphs and get our Life article in Nature? To the fearful, religious, self-serving or altruistic, the more pertinent questions might be: “What can I do in This Life to enhance my/others’ Afterlife chances?”. To some religious people, the questions might be: “How much good do I have to do/how much bad stuff must I not do/how many rules must I obey[/not break] until I can get to the Best Afterlife/Heaven/escape this cycle of Lives/see that it’s all an illusion anyway/Nirvana”.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Would you like to be the smartest person at math?
Answer: Haha, no. I seem to vaguely remember wanting to be smartest at something when I was a little kid, or maybe just one of the smartest. But you grow up and get wiser. Here are the four valuable lessons that helped me to do that and, in that process, helped me to become much happier. The first lesson is that being smartest at maths is like being best at anything else. Every time you’re best in some group, you get elevated to a higher league, where you get to compete with a smaller but smarter or more talented group of people. After this happens a few times, you realise that there are many leagues above you to conquer, like climbing a mountain with intermediate peaks ascending into the cloudy unknown heights. You realise that it will be a long climb, and if you really want to get the top and be the very smartest person at maths in the world, then it means beating seven billion other people, which is not very likely. I wasn’t born a genius or anything, and others were. The second lesson is that the rewards and praise for being best gradually get replaced by demands and expectations. If you’re really good at something, then you might get encouragement and praise to begin with but, as you turn that talent into good grades or, later, a high-level career, then your talents - and hard work - are expected, and the expectations steadily rise. From the first lesson, you hopefully learned some humility, knowing that you’ll never be the very smartest, but even being really smart at what you do is no longer that great. It can often feel mostly like hard and stressful work - because it is. Still, you should be grateful and happy for all that your talent, hard work and lots of luck have granted you, and I am. Luckily, my work is the reward itself, and is not just hard work and stress but also a source of deep meaning and contentment. The third lesson was particularly important for me. I learned this at M.I.T. where I spent the first year of my PhD studies. I was really nervous to go there, thinking that most of my fellow PhD students would be far smarter than me. I did meet a few alien-smart students but, to my surprised relief, most students were just very smart and very hard-working. I did as well as most of them (though many later passed me by), perhaps due to good Scandinavian education, not having to teach unlike most other students, and to high levels of panic that drove me hard. This taught me that I might not be the smartest but I was smart enough. But that was not the main lesson here. My supervisor at M.I.T. was the legendary Gian-Carlo Rota, often called the father of combinatorics. He was endlessly generous and supportive, and had created not only major subfields of mathematics but, through his never-ending initiatives and paternal care, had also cultivated a whole community of mathematicians to populate these subfields. He was a fascinating, brilliant, wise and lovely person who I highly admired. But it struck me that he was not a genius at maths, only very very good, and with sustained and heroic efforts, my good but not-genius talents might also let me become a leader of maths, if hardly at his level. But, instead of motivating me to work even harder, this realisation instead led to a far more important realisation, and one which tore down my childhood vainglory: Gian-Carlo Rota was overall a happy person but he had paid a steep price for his dedication to maths, with next to no life beyond his vocation. I realised that being the smartest or best was not worth the price: standing on top of the mountain is lonely and cold, and finding balance in life would be wiser. For me, at least. So now, I am happy to be very good at maths and at my work, at least good enough to do what I need to do, and good enough to let me grow at the pace of those rising expectations. Half of my colleagues are far smarter than me, and that is fine with me. I feel pride on their and our school’s behalf, especially when they achieve something particularly impressive. What makes this pride on their behalf particularly easy for me is what I learned from the fourth lesson: no-one in the world is best. You might be better than everyone else at something, say throwing a heavy object the furthest. That might give you a shiny medal but doesn’t mean that you’re any better than anyone else at anything else. Each of us is good at some things and bad at others, and I mostly like my spread of talents. I’m very good at a few things, ok at many things, sadly terrible at too many things, and happily terrible at a few selected things, including half my hobbies. I’m better at many things than my far smarter colleagues, and they are far better at other things than me too. Our different skill sets are not in competition; instead, they let us help each other in each our complementary ways, in research, in teaching and in general.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Did you ever have a foreign professor in college whose accent was so pronounced that you could not understand the class lecture? What did you do?
Answer: I am sometimes such a professor. My English accent is Australian with added flavours, and many of my international students struggle to understand me. Luckily, they are awesome and brave, and sometimes tell me when they don’t understand me or ask me to speak slower. To help them better understand me, I try to make my accent more neutral; I try to not speak too quickly; I repeat important information in different ways, through allegories, pictures, and videos; I provide extensive written material for all course content; my lectures are all recorded; and I subtitle all my YouTube videos. These measures seem to make our communication work well, and I’m grateful for my students’ brave feedback that lets me know when they need more help to understand me.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Considering there is so much math out there, is there a point where we stop funding research?
Answer: You might not realise it - most people don’t, not even many mathematicians - but we’re in the middle of the Golden Age of Mathematics, with more and better maths being produced than ever before in history. All this maths has massive enabling potential: think of AI or machine learning or data science or cryptography or computer science or just about any other recent technologies or logistical advances, and you’ll find that maths is central to what makes it all work. And due to its long sustainability and broad versatility, maths never has a used-by-date and it can keep finding new uses. These factors make maths one of the best-yielding longterm investments that society could make. Similarly, most big companies, regardless of industry, would be wise to employ at least a couple of mathematicians. But despite the wealth of quality maths being produced these days, the demand loudly outstrips the supply. We need far more maths, and far more mathematicians. Maybe, one day, we won’t need much more maths, or maybe maths will be generated by AI systems and won’t need as much research funding. But that day is far in the future, and, for now, the meager funding that maths does get is far too small.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Was Mathematics designed to torture people?
Answer: Thanks for a funny and interesting question! Silly as the question sounds, it actually leads to some deep and fundamental aspects of mathematical culture and thinking. Mathematicians often disagree, sometimes vehemently, about the nature of maths (is it a construct or is it real? is it an art or it a science?) and about the value of mathematical results: do you admire a theorem because it took years of heroic effort to prove, resulting in endless pages that only five people in the world can understand? Or do you see more value in simple, elegant and beautiful explanations that can surprise and delight a broad audience? Does maths have intrinsic value or does its value derive from its applications? These and other cultural dichotomies make maths a varied and changing cultural phenomenon. Maths is a hard subject to master and to practise but when cultural values favour strictness and heroic effort, then poor students of maths might face unreasonable burdens. I care about my students and try to make maths as accessible to my students as possible, even very hard maths, and to help them to independently explore and discover beautiful and fascinating maths. But I have older colleagues whose teaching philosophies were different: maths was a heroic endevour that only the talented and resilient few could proudly master. They were proud of the hard and even abusive maths lessons that they themselves endured, and they wanted to impart the same lessons on their own students. Trial by fire; sift away the weak; what doesn’t kill you only makes you stronger: these, together with the romantic tales of the past and glorious heroes of maths, were the values of those colleagues. Now also add sexism and racism of the old Australian culture that many of my colleagues were part of. That culture also instilled scorn for teaching and students, as opposed to noble Research. What you then got was that it wasn’t only the maths lessons that were intentionally hard on students; it was also the academic behaviours and attitudes towards students. Only a decade ago, I frequently heard otherwise lovely colleagues shouting angrily at foreign students for not immediately understanding explanations (given in unfamiliar Australian accents), and to witnessing condescending and patronizing comments made to and about nearly every talented female student. I’m happy to since have seen many say that times have led to happy improvements in our mathematical culture. Unfortunately, I can’t say the same about mathematical education. The tough and nasty attitudes might be gone but they have been replaced by new tortures, like the dumbing down of school maths curricula, the over-emphasis on assessments, and the often counter-productive insistence on cross-disciplinary learning. All this has made maths not only hard but boring to learn, and not rarely meaningless. Unlike the old intentional tortures, these present tortures are not intentional but they might inflict more suffering. Certainly, the numbers of high school students choosing to learn higher maths has steadily decreased over the last two decades. I hope that most school students might one day have the joy of learning maths for the fun and challenge of it, just as I did and just as (I hope) my own uni students do.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: How do you explain what a "vector space" is for a non-math student?
Answer: You can think of vector spaces as coordinate systems or grids or crystal structures. Grids and crystals can have many different types of shapes and symmetries but vector spaces are limited to symmetries that are straight, like straight lines and flat surfaces. Vector spaces also have even spacing, like the numbers on a ruler. The angles in vector spaces are allowed to be crooked, as in a parallelogram: its edges are still straight (and parallel) but the angles are no longer 90 degrees. Those are the main and defining properties of vector spaces, simple enough but also free enough to allow weird and wonderful geometries with many dimensions, not just two or three. What’s the purpose of vector spaces?, you might ask. One answer is that if you can show that some geometry that you’re looking at is a vector space, then you suddenly know a whole lot about that geometry because vector spaces have very strict structures and symmetries, as well as many other properties that mathematicians have shown are true for all vector spaces. You can then also describe and transform your geometry easily, in terms of coordinates and linear functions.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Can I complete my PhD before 30?
Answer: Thanks for asking! I’d wish that I could just answer “Yes! Of course!” but that might not be true. One the positive sides, you seem talented, and you’re about a decade away from 30, so your prospects are good overall. On the less happy sides, you live in Bangladesh where it might be difficult and time-consuming to obtain PhD scholarships. Please keep trying, however, and 30 is very far from now! (And harmless: I know students who have completed their PhDs in their 60s.)

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: What is the best age to be as an adult?
Answer: The answer is surprisingly clear: as an average person (in most not-poor countries), you are fairly and increasingly happy up to roughly 20–25 years of age, and then ok happy but possibly less happy until your turn 35 or so. But then your happiness crashes and burns steadily until you are 55 or so, after which you again can count (on average) on getting steadily happier. There are many cultural and historical factors to take into account here, but the trends are aligned, at least in most non-poor countries: kids are increasingly happy, as their skills, social value and independence grow, but then responsibilities hit, and life gets heavy. Worse still, you then achieve your goals and dreams, and then you lose purpose and hope, and face the existential crisis of wondering what all the effort was for. At that point, you probably have kids and a frayed romantic relationship, and a responsibility-heavy job, and you’re maybe [feeling?] less physically attractive, and your close friends might be off the radar with their own problems. And so on. It’s a tough time, and often a shit time, though you might notice an increase in influence and power due to your experience and possible expertise and leadership. In any case, the statistics are clear: from your first real mid-life crisis around the 35 year mark or so, there is a dismal desert until you’re actually and reliably happy again, around the 55–60 year mark. Of course, you might buck the trend, or be really happy now and then in the interim, but these are the average stats. However, after that long downturn, however, you are less burdened by the stresses, aims, and responsibilities of your early years, and you can then look forward to a steady and even linearly upwards line of happiness. Looking at life as a whole, your adult life is best when you are 80 or older. That’s a long time to wait, so it might be worth highlighting the early happiness of youth: up till 25 or so. Enjoy youth, if possible. But life is also good between 55 and 80. Of course, all of these numbers are averages, and although they are fairly precise averages, they don’t necessarily reflect your particular circumstances. This was all statistics and general life advice. Let’s supplement this with a-personal and realist angle: I would have to say that life is best at my exact age (45) right now, or at least within a year ago, and the best time of life might be right now too. Life has been a wild roller coaster of ups and down and unexpected sideways adventures, and I often feel quite worn out and frazzles by the twists and turns. But it’s also been a life full of purpose, love, loss, achievement, failure, adventure, interest, despair, depression, hope, success, and much more. In the hindsight of memory, happiness, loss and so much more, what in life was good and what was bad? It’s very hard to tell, and most experiences and actions have been both. I try to do and be good but often fail, and I try to experience my life as good, but things are more complicated - and more interesting and beautiful - than what we can see through the topics of simple best/worst metrics. Do your best, enjoy life, both the pain and the pleasure, and don’t expect your life to turn out as you expect it to. But it’s not all chaos and fate either: you can do your part, and you don’t need to be an asshole. Act with goodwill and humility, towards those around you and those around the world. That might make you (and others) happy, also in the long term.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Is being a professor the most relaxed job in the world?
Answer: I couldn’t help laughing out loud to read this question - it really took me by surprise. Professors are insanely busy and often insanely stressed. We work far more and far harder than other people do in comparable jobs outside of academia, for sometimes far less (though still good) pay. We work most evenings and weekends, and the responsibilities and deadlines drive us to frequent sleep deprivation, stress, panic, failure, and periodic breakdowns and depression, all of which we (unhealthily) accept as part of the job. I technically have (lovely and supportive) bosses and (unlovely and oppressive) uni benchmarks but I’m in reality self-driven, answering mostly to my students and their satisfaction with my teaching, and to my CV that is hungry for more quality research publications, successful grant applications, thesis students supervised, journal editing served, refereeing completed, outreach initiatives volunteered, new collaborations cultivated, administration and leadership contributed, course and teaching development designed and created, industry and government bodies consulted, students and colleagues supported and mentored, and endless random daily problems solved. The insane workloads are offset by luxurious autonomy and flexibility. Being a mathematician, I can often work from home or on the beach, and I can take time off and catch up later. I get to teach and support thousands of awesome students, a real joy, and my research gives me the satisfaction of accomplishment. There is an abundance of purpose and meaning in this job, and joy and contentment too. When I am technically on holiday, I often feel like doing my research or other work, often because it’s the sort of interesting stuff that I would do for fun anyway: research, thinking, random creative projects. Come to think of it, being a professor is very much like being an entrepreneur with your own company. You are your own boss and that means freedom but it also means carrying all the responsibility, having to take care of everything yourself, and having your work take over your life. So, is it the most relaxed job in the world? No, pretty much the opposite. I might be lying in bed or on my office sofa while doing my work, and this is nice and relaxing indeed, but it’s hectic and hard, and sometimes too much. I don’t know any of my colleagues who aren’t overworked too, but we’re used to it and, to us, it’s a fine price to pay for all the awesome parts of our job.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: According to religion, we're supposed to be God's best creation. What's his worst?
Answer: The unicorns. They were the most beautiful of all His creations, and thus also His greatest failure. That beautiful spiralling horn on their forehead made it nearly impossible for unicorns to graze; it was just too long. Unicorns therefore starved to death, and since they were close to immortal, it took them an agonisingly long time to die.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Does having a deep understanding of mathematics make you a smarter person than most?
Answer: Yes, of course. You reached that deep understanding through a whole lot of brain training and accumulated wisdom and experience. Training your brain so much made you smarter, and smarter than most. Deep understanding of maths provides you with lots of mental skills that allow you to see further and deeper in the patterns and connections of things, and can give you both clarity, vision, truthfulness and creativity beyond that of most people. You can even measure this to some extent, just like you can measure how fast an athlete can improve their running speed through training: through studying undergraduate maths, my IQ increased from 140 to 170 (and presumably collapsed after my studies). And, of course, not at all. Being smart at maths is only of many ways in which you can be smart. Even though maths gives you important general skills that you could use far beyond maths, most mathematicians don’t actually do that (which seems to me a great waste). And when you train something very hard, you might often neglect to train something else. While I was getting smarter at maths (and IQ-tests), I was also getting worse at writing essays; my social skills deteriorated badly, as did my general common sense. I definitely wasn’t getting smarter, overall. So maths by itself doesn’t make you smarter. But combine maths skills with other ways of thinking, and you might get overall smarter. Just like doing balanced exercise makes you fitter, a balanced training of your thinking, feeling and interacting will make you smarter. Sort of obvious, really, but when it comes to intelligence and IQs and maths, a lot of mythology and wrong ideas confuse even the smartest.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Why is having a PhD much less impressive than it used to be?
Answer: This is because there are far more people getting PhD degrees these days. In the US, for instance, there were roughly 185.000 people who achieved their PhD degree last year, in contrast to only 125.000 people who achieved theirs fifteen years ago. Half a century ago, it was only half that, about 60.000. Of course, the size of the US has grown too but taking that into account tells a similar story: in 1969, roughly 1 of 3400 people achieved their PhD degree; in 2004, it was 1 of 2400, and last year it was 1 of 1800. People are getting more high-level education these days, it would seem. However, a closer look at the numbers reveals just who those people are. Up until the early 2000s, the number of men getting their PhD degree had been declining steadily but then these numbers increased from 65.000 in 2004 to 85.000 in 2012 where it has since steadily remained. That is a big increase but is nothing compared to the dramatic rise in numbers of women who achieve their PhD degrees. Fifty years ago, virtually no women were getting high-level education in the US: 6.000, or 1 of 17.000 women. After a steady increase over the last fifty years, there are now more women achieving their PhD degrees than men in the US: last year there were 100.000 women, and just 85.000 men. The proportion of women getting their PhD degrees is in fact ten times larger than it was fifty years ago. So, women have been gaining access to higher education and have seized these opportunities. But that still only tells half the story. An even closer look at the numbers reveals that half of the PhD-achievers are international students, predominantly from Asia and India. Their numbers have also steadily climbed during the last decade or two as India, China and other Asian nations have grown richer. In other words, there are more and more people getting their PhD degrees in the US, and more women, but fewer Americans overall, and far fewer American men. That might be worrisome but it’s awesome to see that so many more people can now get top-level education. The previously high barriers to education - gender, poverty, and politics - have been significantly lowered, and that’s a really happy thing to see. On the other hand, since there is no comparable increase in academic positions, the competition for those jobs is getting fierce - but that’s another story for another time. A few random sources: U.S. higher education - number of doctoral degrees 1950-2029 | Statista Demographic history of the United States - Wikipedia PhD Study in the USA - A Guide for 2019 | FindAPhD.com

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Besides school, where is mathematics mainly used?
Answer: In all the best jobs and in general everyday life. We are in the middle of a job revolution where jobs require more and more high-level skills, like independent thinking, abstraction, creativity, critical thinking, clarity, and the ability to solve problems and pick up new specific skills on your own. Since those skills are exactly what (real) maths trains you to do, it is not surprising that the top-ranked jobs are overwhelmingly mathematical. That’s been true for a while now but a newer development is that actual maths is also creeping into the jobs of doctors, lawyers, jewelry makers, and countless other jobs that have traditionally been seen as non-mathematical. At the same time, jobs that require less high-level thinking are being taken over by robots and AI, and this process is speeding up. These processes are similarly happening for much of our interaction with our world and each other today: we need to be increasingly literate and numerate, and too few are both. In other words, if you want a decent job and a good life, then learn and practice maths and mathematical thinking. Unfortunately, the maths that is usually taught in school is a sad excuse for real maths education. Learning stuff off by heart and passing tests is pretty much the opposite to learning how to think - you could even call it anti-maths or negative learning. Luckily, there are plenty of resources to help you train your maths brain, for instance by having fun trying to solve maths problems at Brilliant.org, Parabola, Project Euler and elsewhere. This will make you quickly good at a lot of maths - but don’t forget the basics: arithmetic, fractions, basic algebra. If you take care of the easy basics and harder fun stuff, then you’ll quickly get good. And as a bonus, you’ll find the boring and useless school maths really easy.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Where's the beauty in proof by mathematical induction?
Answer: The principle of induction proofs is beautiful and fascinating in itself, like watching dominoes fall. To reach infinity, you only need to count 1, 2, and then you’re there (eventually). In practice, some induction proofs are ugly; others are beautiful. Induction is a powerful tool in maths so it is used a lot, also when much prettier proofs exist. For instance, if I were to ask you to prove that 1 + 2 + ⋯ + n = 1 2 n ( n + 1 ) , then you might be tempted to use induction when you could have looked for some of the really beautiful proofs of this identity. On the other hand, some my favourite proofs are by induction, like Shelah’s proof of the Hales-Jewitt Theorem or Erdős and Rado’s simple proof of their beautiful Sunflower Lemma.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Where and how should I publish my proof of the Riemann hypothesis?
Answer: Thanks for asking! There are several significant hurdles on the way to getting your proof published. The first and biggest is that your proof is almost certainly wrong. Solving the Riemann conjecture has defeated tens of thousands of professional mathematicians working in collaboration over the last 160 years. That you, working on your own, should succeed where they failed together is highly unlikely. It is far more likely that you have overlooked some flaw in your proof. That said, it is often possible to find some new maths that has been overlooked by everyone else, and an outsider’s fresh perspective can sometimes help. The next hurdle is that no-one will believe you even if your proof is correct. If you send your article to a research journal, then the editors will almost certainly dismiss it out of hand. As an editor myself (for instance of Parabola), I frequently receive articles from non-professional mathematicians who claim to have solved some big conjecture. Unlike many other editors, I don’t immediately dismiss these submissions - but the proofs always turn out to be wrong, and it sometimes feels like wasted time and effort to spot the inevitable errors. Next, there is the hurdle of presentation. You might be surprised to hear that mathematical research is a cultural game. It even follows fashions and trends, and I have several times had my research be rejected from top journals because it was about topics that would not be of sufficient interest to readers. That is perfectly fair and reasonable. This social bias plays an important non-cultural role too: mathematicians rely on truth, and if your topic is fashionable, then there will be more expert referees available to assess your work, which means that the journal can be more confident in the quality and integrity of its contents. This principle extends to the way in which you present the article. As a non-mathematician, you would probably write up your results in a way that stood out as rough and contrasting to professionally written maths that is beautifully written in L A T E X and following standard mathematical conventions of presentation. This would raise red flags to editors: if you are not even able to present your work professionally, then what is the chance that your maths is professional? Again, your maths might be 100% correct but editors are busy and rely on those red flags to filter away the low-quality submissions. Also, editors expect submitted articles to be in (nearly) publishable shape: rough drafts are a waste of everyone’s time. Finally, there is you. That sounds really harsh, and it is. Everyone can join the happy game of maths research, and non-professional mathematicians can contribute greatly and importantly. For instance, one of the Polymath Projects was in large part successful due to the insights of a high school maths teacher, working alongside some of the best professional mathematicians, including Terry Tao. However, mathematics is a meritocracy that cuts both ways: you can get acknowledged and applauded for your work regardless of who you are - but your work is also how you are measured. If you haven’t previously published good maths research, then editors might have biased reservations against you. That is partly fair: the likelihood of your submitted research being good is greater if you have previously demonstrated great work. But it is also unfair (and unmeritorious): your work should ideally be judged on its own, not by your previous work. That lends particularly unfair bias against PhD students and other early career researchers, and might sometimes allow renowned researchers to publish sub-par work. In your case, it is also both fair and unfair. Editors should ideally judge your work but, in reality, your lack of demonstrated quality research only adds to the pile of red flags that those busy editors will see raised. I am sorry if this all sounds daunting and depressing to read - but please don’t give up! One way to see this in a positive light is that you are striving towards perhaps the greatest goal that maths presently taunts us with. Such a great achievement deserves equally great effort, and a few cultural and presentational hurdles are nothing compared to having solved the Conjecture. And knowing what those hurdles are might help overcome them. So what can you do right now? You should check your proof again, this time with the assumption that it is wrong. Try to break it as hard as you can, leaving no tiny detail or explanation unturned. If your proof survives, then learn L A T E X (it’s worth learning anyway!) and look up mathematical research articles on the Riemann hypothesis to try to emulate the style and quality of those articles. Then, having made a decent draft, try to find a professional expert on the Riemann Hypothesis who might be willing to assess your proof and give you detailed advice on how to proceed. Good luck!

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: How does a PhD from Harvard differ from a PhD from MIT? Who seems more knowledgeable and hard worked?
Answer: The PhD degrees from Harvard and from MIT are equally excellent, partly because Harvard and MIT enjoy very close collaboration, and students from either university can study a wide range of courses at the other through their cross registration agreements. Each has its different strengths, however, with MIT being nearly unrivaled in STEM areas, and Harvard leading the pack in business, law, and humanities. They both excel in medicine and together they host the Harvard-MIT Program in Health Sciences and Technology. Although Harvard and MIT are separate and sometimes very different in style and areas of expertise, they are nevertheless within walking distance of each other and are sometimes seen as one hugely impressive university, with greater impact than most nations. A PhD from either is usually top-tier.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: As a child or teenager, did you or fellow students ever do something that made your teacher break down into tears in the classroom?
Answer: My favourite episode in this vein was when I was 14 or so. One day, one of our teachers got really angry at a girl in my class for some trivial but forgotten reason, and roughly shoved my classmate’s desk into her stomach, leaving my classmate winded. That only lasted a second or so though. Recovering, my classmate calmly looked our teacher in the eye and, without a word, gave her the biggest punch to the jaw. Our teacher burst into tears and ran out of the room, and we burst into laughter. After a few minutes of waiting for our teacher to return, one girl went out to find her and returned to inform us that our teacher was outside the door, waiting for us to come out and apologise, which of course we didn’t. Instead, we enjoyed happy freedom for the rest of the hour. Maybe not nice of us but we’d won this particular battle.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: What do teachers think of teaching a beautiful female teen?
Answer: I know this isn’t what the question was fishing for - but here’s my answer anyway. As a teacher, I mostly react to beautiful female students with caution, empathy, and possible compassion. Why? Because (university) classes are sometimes really large, often between 200–500 students in one auditorium, and because my most of my students are male. It’s tough being a woman student in these male dominated environments, where men can outnumber women by as much as 24 to 1 (in engineering). Even though a lot of old misogynist culture has been cleaned up, there is still lots of overlooked microaggression, and occasional overt sexist abuse still occurs, still here and there prevalent and promoted. Many women are told throughout their lives that they aren’t as suited to mathsy subjects as men, and there are still old-school professors who sometimes think this too. It’s no wonder that so many of my female students feel far less confident about their maths abilities than their male classmates, and studies sadly show that tutors and lectures mark with often subconscious bias against female students. This is despite countless studies showing that maths is 100% gender-neutral - but culture is stuck hard in the rut on this issue. But tough as it is to be a woman student, it can be doubly tough to be a beautiful woman student. Here, the myths multiply. Not only are you a woman and therefore unlikely to be good at maths; you probably also use your beauty to gain unfair advantages. You have to face hundreds of fellow students staring at you each day, some of whom will get crushes on you, perhaps even stalk you. If you relax and are just yourself, let your guard down, then this might be taken as flirt, and then people might slam your for being a tease. And all those crushing on you and get rejected might not take it well; after all, many students haven’t mastered emotional maturity yet (for that matter, that is also true of many much older people). That could include close friends. So, when I see a beautiful woman among my students, I try to create extra space and support for her, at least until I can see that she is at ease. She might suspect me of being a creep, which is a natural worry if you’ve previously met creeps among your professors. And she might be worried that I prejudge her as stupid, which also happens, sadly. If those barriers can be overcome, then there is room to encourage and help her gain confidence in her own abilities, if she hasn’t got that already. By repeatedly emphasising to the class that we are all in it together to help each other learn, a group vibe can be created where everyone can join in, regardless of genders and looks. I’m really proud of my students here at UNSW that this group vibe occurs far more often than not. I should add that I try to put every one of my students at ease, and support and encourage them, not just the beautiful women among them. Nor do all, or even most, beautiful women students necessarily face the burdens described above. I have however seen too many of these students looking particularly hunted and haunted. It shouldn’t be this way, and I’ve seen it be far less of a problem elsewhere, for instance in Northern Europe, where women generally have far more social freedom and far fewer obstacles and abuses than here in Australia. Things are improving though, if slowly.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Why does God say that homosexuality is wrong? What is wrong about two people of the same sex loving each other?
Answer: The short answer: God didn’t mind homosexual love but then things got messy. The long answer: God gets jealous when His humans love anyone or anything other than Him. Remember when Adam and Eve fell in love and forgot to worship God? That made Him feel hurt, rejected and angry. And betrayed: Adam and Eve had made themselves into tiny competitor-gods, creating new life through sex and agriculture. That was no way to thank Him for the Paradise that He had given Him, He thought, and He struck out in anger and hurt, condemning his Humans to suffer all the pains and evils of the world. If only Adam and Eve had just been homosexual and of the same sex, then they would not have become as mini-godly, and God might not have felt quite as betrayed. They might not have been cast out of paradise, and Eve certainly wouldn’t have to endure the pains of pregnancy, birth and child-raising. But God meant to hurt his Humans, and we have ever since been bound to a cycle of pain. To begin with, He wanted his Humans to feel that pain, so He forbade any attempts to escape it, for instance by finding homosexual love in order to escape pregnancy and birth pains. Later, He forgave us but, by then, He had discovered that it is nice with lots of worshipers. So, instead of ending our pain, He let those pains continue. (*) That says just about everything about God’s emotional immaturity and about His egotistical “love” that He has for his Human. Thank God, He’s been been out of the picture the last two thousand years - but damn Him for not relieving us of the pains that He inflicted on us. That would have been the decent thing to do. The very long answer: Read here. (*) To be fair, He did later tell us through His Son that it was now ok to ignore the old Laws, including the Law forbidding homosexuality. Now, the only law was to love Him and to love each other. He was feeling sentimental and sorry at the time, deeply missing his Humans, but they had moved on from that toxic relationship. He soon moved on too. Ironically, this attracted many more Humans to worship Him (in His absence) and they internalized all His old and hurtful Laws. It was (and is) a Lose-Lose situation: in absentia, He benefits nothing from His Human’s love and worship, and they torture and restrict themselves without reward.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: How can students cope with professors that lecture in thick accents?
Answer: Pay attention, listen, and try to understand your lecturer’s mannerisms and ways of thinking. Look at your lecturer’s body language and try to lip-read. Look at the lectures slides and material so that you know the context and message of what your lecturer is saying. It all helps, and there are many other ways to help you cope with thick accents. This is a problem that my many and awesome international students have to suffer. They are generally excellent at written English but are not used to the sometimes thick Australian accents that us lecturers inflict on them, here at UNSW. My accent is reasonably neutral but is still often very different from what my students are used to hearing. To help my students better understand what I am saying, I provide them with heaps written material and make sure that my lectures are recorded, so that they can revisit and rewind the lectures. I also make YouTube videos of tutorial questions and make sure to include subtitles. I encourage students to email or message me whenever they have questions or comments, and I create online course platforms like Facebook Group, Moodle, Piazza, Edstem, etc. so that we can all communicate and contribute together, happily and productively. Accents and occasional broken English really don’t have to be a problem.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Have the Danes stopped laughing yet, or are they concerned that The Trumpster may decide not to nuke the hurricane but nuke Greenland instead?
Answer: The Danes have moved on to new entertainment and don’t fear much in general, not even Trump’s craziness. As for nuking Greenland, the US has done that already. In 1968, a US B-52 carrying four nuclear hydrogen bombs crashed into the ice-covered ocean near the US air base at Thule in Greenland. One of the bombs’ TNT detonated and scattered the bombs and their plutonium over a 7.7 km² (3 square miles) area of ice, causing widespread nuclear contamination, and the other parts sunk beneath the ocean, causing even worse contamination as plutonium and other highly poisonous and radioactive elements were dispersed by ocean currents and ocean food chains. One bomb was never found and lies underwater, a literal ticking time bomb of further radiation. These bombs were part of US nuclear programs during the Cold War. One program was to have a dozen planes, armed with nuclear weapons, to circulate in the airspace close to USSR, at the ready to deploy. Another program, which was ended prematurely by the Thule accident, was to secretly store 600 nuclear weapons under the Greenland ice. At the time, the Kingdom of Denmark was officially a nuclear-free zone (and still is) but its government had made secret (and illegal) agreements with the US to allow nuclear weapons to be stocked and flown to Thule. If the Danish public were to know of these facts, then there would be massive outrage, and the Danish government would have to step down. Therefore, the government kept a heavy lid on the affair, as did the US who wanted their military secrets to be kept secret. That might have been difficult to do. Later investigations have uncovered that more than 400 of the Greenlanders and Danes, and an unknown number of American soldiers, who cleaned up the accessible parts of the radiated ice later died from cancer that was directly due to the severe radiation poisoning. Greenlanders were for a long time prohibited from hunting and fishing in a wide area around Thule; that would presumably also have caused rumours and speculation to spread. How many Greenlanders have died from the radiation through air, water and food is not known. It was nearly three decades later, in 1995, that a particularly insightful, fearless and stubborn Danish journalist, Poul Brink, managed to uncover these facts and then succeeded to make them public. Since then, other investigations have been conducted, including a larger one by the BBC. Public outrage at these scandals did happen, and the 1700 surviving victims of the cleanup were shortly each awarded 50kkr, roughly 9000USD at the time. The Thule Air Base is still operational and important to the US, who two years ago spent $40M to upgrade its radar system. References: United States Department of State, Nuclear Accidents at Palomares, Spain in 1966 and Thule, Greenland in 1968, Historical Research Project No. 1421 (2010), 48 pages. [declassified in 2013] Eric Schlosser, Command and Control, Penguin Books, 2014, 656 pages. J. Dragsdahl, The Danish Dilemma, Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists, Vol. 57 (2001), pp. 45–50. More references, including to scientific studies of the radiation levels and effects, can be found here and here. An excellent film, The Idealist, presents a gripping portrayal of Poul Brink’s investigation.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: What is God's answer to suffering?
Answer: According to the Bible, He has variously answered: “Yeah, suffer!!!” and “I’m soooo sorry; please accept this bribe and love me again!!!” He was always emotionally immature and deeply insecure, which is why He and His humans got into such a toxic and abusive relationship. They didn’t help matter either: soon after each new honeymoon period of worship, prosperity and happiness, they took Him for granted, neglected Him and started worshiping themselves, their riches, and even other gods. Each time that happened, He struck out in pain and rage, and made His humans suffer as much as He could. But poor God never could stay alone and lonely for long, so He always came crawling back, begging for forgiveness. It took four thousand years for God and His humans to finally break up. His last-ditch and desperate attempt was to send His Son as a sign of His love and as a sort of relationship and communications counselor - but it was too late, and His humans had moved on. That was two thousand years ago, and He hasn’t been seen since. Let’s hope that it stays that way, both for our sake and His.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Why do PhD thesis advisors sometimes allow a student to defend even though they are not ready?
Answer: Often because they are bad thesis advisors. I have friends who had such bad advisors. It was tragic to see those friends confidently submit and defend their theses, full of relief and pride, only to be crushed and defeated by the (kind but fair) thesis referees. In one instance, we were waiting outside the closed-room PhD defense of one friend, with champagne, food and excitement. This friend emerged four hours later, ashen and shaking: the referees could not accept the thesis. My friend could choose between yet another year of research, in the hope of adding enough thesis content to get it passed, or to give up and accept a Masters degree instead. I’m proud of my friend for choosing the hard extra year. Another friend had a similar traumatic experience; it took him years to get over. In these cases, the thesis advisor should not let the student submit their thesis. Sometimes, it is not really the advisor’s fault: maybe the student has run out of time or didn’t properly communicate with their advisor or just went off the rails; or maybe there is a difference in academic cultures of the advisor and the referees. But, sometimes, the advisor is fully at fault. I have even seen (in areas outside of my own) schools accepting too many and too weak students into the PhD program in order to get cheap lab and teaching staff. In such cases, those poor students often get neglected by their advisor and by their school, and by the time that they must submit, they are far from ready to do so; they might never be. This is abusive exploitation and it makes me sad and angry. Luckily, this seems to happen in only few areas, and luckily never, as far as I have seen, in my area (maths).

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Why doesn't someone having a PhD impress you?
Answer: Getting a PhD is hard. Even getting into PhD studies is pretty hard and requires years of dedication and hard work. But getting a PhD is just the first and easiest step in an academic career. After having climbed more of those steps, you look back and are no longer impressed. And then there’s life. Life is hard, sometimes far harder than a PhD. Raising kids, for instance, is far harder than a PhD, roughly 3–5 PhD’s worth of work and stress per kid. That’s a worthy achievement and very impressive, especially if you and your partner don’t break under the strain and split up. Every second person achieves this, and yet no-one makes a big fuss about them, nor gives them fancy awards and cool letters to prefix their names by. When someone has spent four years of PhD studies and gets their degree, they are celebrated and admired. When a mom has spent four years in pregnancy, breastfeeding and sleep deprivation, she is usually not celebrated or admired, especially not if she is achieving it by all herself. That seems unfair but admiration is not always rational, nor compassionate. And, these days, I am not so impressed by big flashy achievements. Once you get to the halfway point in life, you will probably have achieved plenty already. What impresses me much more, these days, is whether you actively strive to become a better person, and one who actually gives a damn. Are you kind and caring, and do you give more than you take, mend more than you destroy? That is real achievement, far harder even than having kids, let alone completing a PhD. I really hope that I’ll one day achieve this.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question:
How can we prove that
√
2
is an irrational number using induction proof (recurrent proof)?
Answer: I am fairly sure that there are no known natural inductive proofs to show that √ 2 is irrational. All known proofs are essentially variations of the standard proof by contradiction. The main obstacle to finding an induction proof that is not also a contradiction proof is that you have just one small integer, not infinitely many of them, and that looking at infinite sequences would presumably involve limits and convergences. Even if each term of such a sequence were irrational, then we couldn’t immediately conclude that the limit would also be irrational, and it would presumably be very hard to provide a proof that would force the limit into being so. However, you can turn these natural contradiction proofs into awkward and unnatural contradiction proofs that (unnecessarily) involve induction, for instance as described here.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Why should high school students learn geometry, trigonometry, and advanced algebra? It seems that these subjects don't have much of a practical application in day-to-day life.
Answer: They shouldn’t. Why? Because it’s really important that students (and everyone else) learn maths. That might sound confusing, so please let me explain. The world is now a place where you need a lot of maths skills. Most of the top-rated jobs involve being some flavour of mathematician, like data scientist, statistician, actuary or software developer. And most well-rated jobs involve increasing amounts of maths, particularly statistics, even doctors and lawyers (to the dismay of some of my doctor friends). Meanwhile, AI and automation are replacing jobs with less need for high-level thinking. However, while jobs are requiring more and more maths skills, there are fewer and fewer people learning those skills. This is a big and growing problem. A similar problem is that we are facing an increasingly complex world and have fewer maths skills with which to navigate it. We therefore need to get smarter, especially at maths skills. But the sort of maths skills that we need these days are generalist skills: to recognise and visualise patterns clearly, to think logically and critically, and to be able to aquire skills and solutions independently and creatively. With those skills, you can quickly pick up specific skills, like some algebra or statistics, or how to code in some language, or to use some particular software. It’s a waste of time to teach those specific skills, not least because the specific skills required by job trends quickly change. You don’t get those generalist skills by the maths that is taught in high schools these days. Geometry would be an excellent way for students to learn to think logically and creatively - but only if it were taught properly. These days, it isn’t, if it’s taught at all: education has been replaced by rote-learning aimed at maximising standardised test scores. The geometry that is now “taught” is a waste of time and resources, and the same is true of calculus, trigonometry, calculus, algebra and, especially, statistics. So what sort of maths do we need to learn? Just like learning to read and write, we need to learn the very basics of maths, like numbers, arithmetic, fractions, and basic algebra, and we need to learn this early on, not stretch it out and forget about it, which is what happens in schools today. Reduce the number of tests and assessments, reduce (or eliminate) the homework load, but raise the bar for those basic skills and do everything to help students get over that bar. It’s vital that students gain basic numeracy but that’s not happening right now: typically, 40% of people in the West are now functionally innumerate. Once basic numeracy has been acquired, we need to focus on independent and creative thinking. Replace rote-learned subjects by puzzles and games that encourage and develop mathematical thinking and creativity. Kids are already doing this, not because they want to learn maths but because they love to play and interact and learn, and playing is one of the best methods that our minds have for learning. When kids play with LEGO or compete with speed-cubing algorithms, or code in Scratch or Minecraft, or even play Clash of Clans, they are very efficiently learning to think mathematically. The maths problems and videos at Brilliant.org, Parabola, Vi Hart, Eddie Woo, and countless other sites are really popular among kids too. These are awesome maths resources and are endlessly better than stale lessons in rote-learned (and quickly forgotten) statistics formulae and calculus methods. Of course, schools (and their political masters) are not going to discard traditional lessons and assessments any time soon, especially not in favour of games. But they should, and I think that they eventually will. Even schools must eventually catch up and provide the sort of education that is now needed. In the meantime, I’m very relieved to see that kids, on the whole, are teaching themselves, which is exactly what is increasingly required of us all. It’s just a tragedy that schools waste their time, rather than help them learn.

Question: Atheists, have God-believing people ever tried to change you?
Answer: Of course, countless times, and I usually enjoy it when they do. The funniest and saddest time that a Christian tried to convert me was a few years ago, at night in a cafe where I met this interesting and pretty woman. That’s what I told her too, but she just laughed and said that my girlfriend needn’t know. That made me laugh in turn but didn’t change my mind, so instead I teased her that here she was, the sinful Christian, trying to both save and corrupt me, the virtuous heathen. She did laugh at that but later started crying at the rejection which made me feel a bit like shit. But an overall happy if messy evening, hopefully for her too. Question: What do Nordic people think of Donald Trump?
Answer: Ok, let’s see. Trump claimed that the Finns rake their forests to prevent wildfires. The Finns thought that this was the funniest thing ever, and they responded with a storm of ridiculing posts and satire videos under the hastag #RakeAmericaGreatAgain. The Swedes were far less amused when Trump kept posting belligerent Twitter messages telling Sweden and its Prime Minister to free the US rapper A$AP Rocky who was detained in Stockholm on charges of serious assault.
