Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Do you think that learning mathematics makes you more intelligent?
Answer: Yes. If you actually learn it, that is. By that, I mean learning to think abstractly, logically, creatively, and independently, not only about arithmetic, geometry, algebra, and so on, but also about everything around you in your life and in your world. Maths is a form of art or sport or meditation, and you get some very strong and versatile brain muscles by practising and getting better at maths. For my part, my undergraduate maths studies boosted my tested IQ from about 130–140 to about 160-170, at least for a while - so I definitely got smarter - but only in certain specific ways, and I almost certainly also grew less intelligent in other ways, like being sociable or writing essays, say, due to lack of practice and a different focus. Sadly, the useful and brain-training type of (real) maths, is not what most school kids get to learn. Instead, rote learning of nearly useless specific maths skills and artificial “real-life” applications are taught, with the aim to make tests and assessments easy to make and mark, and to boost the academic standings of school, districts and even countries. The lack of qualified mathematicians among teachers doesn’t help; nor does it help that administrators create school maths curriculae, not mathematicians. However, I hope that you were lucky to get quality maths education! Don’t worry, though, if you weren’t. There are plenty of ways to learn maths by yourself and thereby get stronger and more creative maths-brain muscles. For instance, check out the brilliant problems at Brilliant.org, Project Euler, Parabola and elsewhere. Good luck, and enjoy!

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: How do irrational numbers exist in real life? And if they don't, what are the implications?
Answer: Some irrational numbers certainly exist in real life. For instance, the circumference of a circle is π times larger than its diameter. If π didn’t exist, then circles and circular motion couldn’t exist. Other irrational numbers appear everywhere in real life too: e appears every time there is some sort of exponentional growth or decay, and the Golden Ratio ϕ enables the beauty and symmetry of Fibonacci-type patterns that you see all around in nature, from flowers to galaxies. We are used to simple irrational numbers like √ 2 and don’t see them as “unnatural”. But that wasn’t always the case. A couple of millenia ago, the Pythagoreans discovered irrational numbers and it shook them to the core. They were a mystic cult of excellent mathematicians who, among other things, worshipped numbers and rational ratios, like 1 : 2 (or 1 2 ), 3 : 5 (or 3 5 ) and so on, which they saw as giving the world divine and beautiful order: musical scales, human relationships, and even the cycles of the planets and stars. Finding out that the world contained √ 2 and other such irrational and heretical disharmonies threw the cult into an existential crisis, and they even ended up murdering one of their own for revealing this disturbing and dangerous fact. This might seem funny to us now - but some of us are still not comfortable with the existence of some numbers, as you can tell by their names: complex, imaginary, irrational, surreal. And today, there are still people who don’t believe that the weirder sort of irrational numbers - the transcendentals - exist, partly because we have found nearly none of them, despite standard maths telling us that there are mindbogglingly many of them. To take this question deeper, we could ask what “to exist” really means. Physics tells us that our reality is very surreal, and possibly not even real in any intuitively meaningful way. Things seems to exist possibly, multibly, fractionally, not at all, randomly, multifacettedly, contradictingly… If existence is indeed a meaningful concept, then there are presumably many ways in which something can exist. Numbers exist as concepts in our minds and they seem to exist in the symmetries and patterns of the world. Some people even say the world is just numbers and maths, though that seems highly unlikely to me. I would really love to know how all the various forms of [non]existence interplay but, even if we knew this, we would probably never really understand it.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: What is an experience you had with a professor you'll never forget?
Answer: So many memorable experiences… The professor who forgot to take his microphone off for his toilet break between lectures. The professor who liked to bully people and once picked a fight with me in public but got so angry by our argument that he couldn’t speak and had to leave the hall. The professors who used to get so drunk at our school parties that they tore up the big potted plants and used them for sword fighting. The professor who joined me and other junior staff in climbing over a fence to have a happy pool party. The professors who were incredibly generous to me, including Peter Cameron, Rosemary Bailey, Micheal Cowling, Catherine Greenhill, Veena Sahajwalla, Carsten Thomassen, Sergey Fomin, Daniel Kleitman, Gian-Carlo Rota, and many others. I have particularly fond memories of Gian-Carlo Rota. I had asked to come and visit him at M.I.T. for informal PhD supervision, and he immediately and warmly agreed. He was just as welcoming in person and went out his way to introduce me to his colleagues and their research projects and to make my girlfriend and me feel welcome and included while we were in Boston. This included taking us out for lunches and dinners. I vividly remember some of them, including one at the Harvard Club and a talk at the National Academy of Arts and Sciences, feeling very young and intimidated. The attending (and half-asleep) members were on average 85 years old and included several Nobel prize winners. These acts of generosity on Rota’s behalf might have been happy and easy for him to enact, and he did seem to genuinely like and find us and our young ideas interesting. However, it made a huge impact on us, and it motivated me even further to work hard and get good and creative research done. I am still very grateful for all that he did for us. He died near the end of my year-long visit and it was a shock to me and everyone else around him, and I wish that there had been more to time get to know him. It’s strange: although it’s a long time ago and a lot of life has happened since, I still miss him.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: What is the definition of ‘proposition’ in mathematics?
Answer: “Proposition” has two different meanings in mathematics. The first is seen in mathematical (and philosophical) logic. Here, a proposition is a statement that can be shown to be either true or false but not both. For instance, “ 2 + 3 = 5 ” and “It is raining” are each propositions, whereas “ 2 + x = 5 ” and “Blue is a nice colour.” are not. It can sometimes be tricky and subtle to tell whether a statement is a proposition: it almost always depends on the context. The second meaning is of a more literary, or book-keeping, kind. Here, “proposition” has a similar function as “figure” or “table”, say. In particular, it describes the formal presentation of a mathematical fact in a paper, book, or talk. The result is given a title “Proposition X”, where X is some number, just like figures and tables are given titles “Figure X” (or Fig. X) and “Table X”. This sort of proposition is also a proposition of the first sense described above. However, it is a special kind of proposition: it is always true, and it has a particular degree of importance. It is quite important, and therefore more important than only slightly important mathematical facts (which are called lemmas) but not as important as mathematical facts that are very important (which are called theorems). The hierarchy of mathematical facts, ordered by importance is something like this: There are also corollaries (facts that follow almost immediately from other facts, and which could be very important, not important at all, or anything in between ), conjectures, comments, questions, problems, and more. These labels help make mathematical text easier to write, to read, and to cite. This reminds me of one of my PhD students who was very bright and very humble. I was often excited by his mathematical discoveries but he played them down, calling them remarks where I saw them to be lemmas, lemmas where I saw propositions, and propositions where I saw theorems. We had many friendly and happy arguments about this.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Is it true that every time a deck of cards is shuffled it is probably in a combination that has never occurred before?
Answer: In the real world, probably no. It is true, as others have written, that the number of permutations of a deck of cards is astronomical. Therefore, if one could shuffle a deck of card in a perfectly random way each time, then each shuffle would almost certainly yield a new permutation. However, unless you throw the cards up in air, and pick them up from the floor, then your shuffling will not be very random. The deck that you buy is ordered, and there is a lot of order among cards that are collected after some given game. Just think of how, after a few games of [insert your favorite card game], the deck gets annoyingly non-random. Now think of how long it takes to sort things. When I mark a couple of hundred test assignments, it takes me at least half an hour just to sort them into alphabetical order. That is not just me being slow; it takes time to sort things. The opposite is just as true: it also takes time to really mess things up. With any orderly (i.e., not throwing the cards in the air) method of shuffling your cards, it would take a long time to properly randomise the deck. Worse still, most orderly methods fall into repeating patterns with short cycle length. It’s actually very hard and time-consuming to construct “real randomness”. Add to this the Birthday Paradox that Alan Martin described in an excellent answer. The question posed is not “Is it true that the next time you shuffle your deck of cards, it will probably be a new one?” - instead, it asks “Is it true that every time [etc.]”. We must therefore compare all shuffles with each other, not just one shuffle with each preceeding shuffle. That is a lot of comparisons, so even though it is quite unlikely (though no longer astronomical, as described above) that a given two shuffles resulted in the same deck order, they nevertheless add up to some perhaps significant probability. A less lazy answer would attempt to roughly estimate this probability. In order to do that, you would need to know the number of deck shuffles and the game played. I won’t do that but will instead conjecture, if we were to look at all the shuffles of regular card decks throughout history so far, that the probability of finding an identical pair of deck permutations is not vanishing; it might even be as “big” as winning a major lottery.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: As a professor, what makes you like a student?
Answer: I like almost all of my students, partly because they are generally awesome (here at UNSW) as people and as students, and partly because they give me great joy by teaching them and seeing them learn and do well. And partly because I feel paternal and protective towards them when they are stressed by the hard content to learn, the too many assignments, tests and exams to pass, their uncertain futures, their turbulent young-people lives (or differently tough mature-age-student lives), and possible cultural challenges, lonelinesses and other burdens. If students like me in return, as a group or as individuals, then there is an additional happy cycle of liking. Even though I am often too busy (and a bit reclusive), it’s always nice when students feel like chatting about some maths or philosophy or anything else that they want to share and discuss, or when they just want to get to know me better. And so on. There are plenty of reasons why I like my students, and almost never any reason not to.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: What are the considerations when a professor decides to improve (or not) a student's grade, when the student is 1-3 points to next grade?
Answer: Fairness and truth. A grade is what it is and can’t be improved (or degraded). But also fairness and compassion. It the exam was too hard or there was some small room for interpretation in the solutions (despite hopefully good and accurate marking schemes), then scaling of marks can happen (though this is a last-resort thing to do if the exam was very poorly set, which should never happen), and natural cut-off levels might be adjusted, so that a cohort of students getting a mark or so from the next grade might be bumped up to the next grade. And administration and compassion. If a student is failing by just a couple marks, and there is room of different interpretations of the solutions, then, for everyone’s sake, you might carefully go through their exam to see whether any solutions could be interpreted, truthfully and fairly but more positively, enough to get the student over the line.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Should everyone in school have to learn advanced math, or does not every student need calculus?
Answer: Almost noone needs to learn calculus - but almost everyone needs to learn maths, including advanced maths. It’s like learning sport or music or art or language. Noone needs to run 100m very quickly or to write yet another essay about The Lord of the Flies. You learn and train to do things like this because they train your brain in various useful ways. In the same way, calculus and other specific maths skills are not of much value in everyday life for most people. However, the learning and training of maths is very useful and important to everyone, to let us train some of our brain muscles that are increasingly important in everyday life and in our careers: abstract thinking, clear vision and logic, curiosity and creativity, and a good sense of proportions and probabilities. This gives us the tools with which to think and evaluate truth on our own, and more and more jobs require this type of thinking. One exception to this general answer is the need for basic skills, like arithmetic. Just as it is really important to learn letters, words, and how to put them well together to form clear and lovely language, it is also really important to know small numbers and be able to do simple arithmetic with them. Unfortunately, most people are taught maths badly. Basic arithmetic is not taught properly in the West, and in both West and East, real maths education of the brain-training type is replaced by test-compatible and superficial “maths”: useless and wasteful rote learning of specific maths skills. Western culture is opposed to maths and other thinking that takes any significant effort; partly therefore, there is a lack of good maths teachers; and school maths curriculae are designed by administrators who have no qualifications nor interest in maths. The result is that up to half of people are functionally innumerate, which makes them more prone to malicious manipulation from advertising, dishonest authorities, and untrue news and memes. In the East, authoritarian and highly competitive cultures squash mathematical independence, inquisitivity, creativity and collaboration. Everywhere, much needless pain and hassle could be avoided with better education, and many lives could be happier, and our societies too. This is a real tragedy. On the brighter side of things, kids want to learn and get better at thinking, and so they are finding ways to train themselves. From thought-provoking YouTube videos to demanding computer games to challenging coding, often all combined together and in community, kids are teaching themselves and each other excellent maths-type thinking skills (though without the arithmetic). This is great to see, even if it does harshly indict our outdated school systems. It’s not surprising either: our kids see the future clearer than we do, and that future requires new skills. Not calculus or other specific old-school skills but general ways of thinking that maths and other brain-training can give you.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Have you ever witnessed a teacher crying and breaking down? What was the cause? Did you or other students or teachers do or say anything?
Answer: This question brings back dark but strangely happy memories, so thanks for asking! :) I have seen many teachers break down, sometimes memorably. Here are a few of the incidents. In 4th grade, we got a lovely and enthusiastic young teacher fresh out of the seminarium. We loved this guy instantly, and this made him go above and beyond for us, teaching us really well and letting us do interesting extracurricular things like leather work, once we had finished our tasks. Sadly, this was back in the old Australian system (early 1980s) where our class would have just one teacher to teach all subjects for the whole year and where culture was unhealthily macho and harsh. These conditions quickly wore our lovely teacher down, and his mood got darker until he wore a permanently red and angry face. We therefore picked on him in small but persistent ways, making him more frustrated and angry, a sad and vicious cycle. It did however generate many episodes that I still find funny. In one, a good mate of mine had hilariously provoked our teacher too much, as often, so my mate was called up to the podium where he had to put out his hand so that our teacher could whack it with his wooden ruler. My cheeky friend pulled away his hand in the last moment and grinned loudly: “Ya missed!!”. Our teacher went particularly beetroot and bugeyed, grabbed my mate’s hand, and put full force into his whack, shouting “I DIDN’T MISS THIS TIME, DID I?!!”. My mate’s hand hurt all day but he didn’t cry (“boys don’t cry”) and was admired by all. A few year later, now in Denmark, my class had a geography and sewing teacher. She was useless as a teacher, partly since she was either retarded or had dementia, not sure which, and we really didn’t like her terrible breath and the spittle flying from her mouth. But we sort of liked her anyway, mostly because she didn’t ask us to do much work. In the sewing lessons, she sometimes flew into rages for no apparent reason, and once started throwing scissors at us (I remember crouching under a table together with another guy). That was unusual and interesting enough behaviour to endear her a little to us. One day, however, one rough and tough classmate calmly called “Miss, could you please help?”. He had been a bit careless and had gotten his left index finger stuck, the sewing machine needle going straight through his nail and flesh to the other side. When our teacher saw what had happened, she flew into yet another rage, shouted incoherently at him and, instead of spooling the needle carefully out of his finger, instead yanked his forcefully hand back, so that the needle tore out through his finger, splitting it. Spurting blood, he seemed shocked but calm, got lots of tissues, and went to the school nurse. His calm reaction won him general admiration from us all (and his finger healed ok). Only now do I wonder whether any of us told any parent or teacher about these sort of incidents: reporting stuff didn’t seem like an option back then. Certainly, she kept teaching us for the rest of the year. My favourite episode in this vein was the year after, when my classmates were 15 or so. One day, one of our teachers got really angry at a girl in my class for some trivial but forgotten reason, and roughly shoved my classmate’s desk into her stomach, leaving my classmate winded. That only lasted a second or so though. Recovering, my classmate calmly looked our teacher in the eye and, without a word, gave her the biggest punch to the jaw. Our teacher burst into tears and ran out of the room, and we burst into laughter. After a few minutes of waiting for our teacher to return, one girl went out to find her and returned to inform us that our teacher was outside the door, waiting for us to come out and apologise, which of course we didn’t. Instead, we enjoyed happy freedom for the rest of the hour. It all seems a bit demented and surreal now but it’s somehow happy memories anyway! :)

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Do professors and teachers give better grades to the students that regularly meet with them?
Answer: I don’t give better grades to students that meet with me regularly - since I aim to be fair and because there is nearly no room for nepotistic influences in their (maths) assessments - but I do admit to caring more about the grades of students who I have come to know. This happens most prominently when I have a stack of assessments to mark. I always get happy when some student does well, and sad when some student does badly, especially if I can tell that they deserved better and just had a bad day. But when I get to the assessment of a student whom I know, then I am anxiously cheering them on as I mark their paper, really hoping that they will do well. Aside from empathy effects, it’s hard to care exactly equally for all people, especially when you have seen close up and in detail how individual people have worked hard to understand and excel. Sometimes, this makes me wonder whether I ever mark some students more favourably than others. Luckily, according to occasional extra checks, I have not yet seen any evidence of this. Maybe, I am lucky to teach and mark maths, and not other subjects - in those, it might be harder to be fair and unbiased.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Mathematicians, how do you shut up a person who claims physics is better than math?
Answer: I’d just say “ok” and leave it at that. Different people have different tastes, and neither field is inherently better than the other. As for which field is “truest” or “most beautiful” or “most applicable”, there are very long and deep and differing philosophical, aesthetic and even religious views.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Do university professors actually enjoy teaching or they would prefer to do research all time?
Answer: When I was a PhD student, I looked forward to being a Researcher, and (naively and arrogantly) saw teaching as not very important, mostly an unfortunate and annoying cost to getting such an academic job. It didn’t help that, to begin with, I was super shy and nervous when teaching, and not very good at it. Over time, though, I got good at teaching, and less shy, and began to enjoy it more and more, until I realised that I enjoyed teaching more than my research. At that point, I began to see myself as both teacher and researcher, and I now really enjoy doing both. These joys complement each other well too. Through teaching, I can help thousands of awesome students to understand and enjoy concepts and to grow and thrive. This, and our happy interaction together, gives me a real kick of intense but short-lived joy. It also supports my research by exciting students to study and conduct research under my supervision. On the other hand, research (in pure maths and applications to non-maths fields) is often slow and hard, and does not give nearly as much intense joy - but instead gives long-lasting and deep satisfaction, as well as research outcomes that I can use in my teaching to excite and inspire my students with. But that’s just me. I have colleagues who love teaching but don’t do research, and I have colleagues who are super-star researchers who dislike and avoid teaching.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Teachers and professors: What was the most satisfying time you busted a student for plagiarism?
Answer: It was when I had given a maths assignment to a graduate class. It was difficult and challenging but also meant to be fun, and I’d given the students several weeks to complete it. When I received the assignment solutions, I saw that many of them were suspiciously similar to each other, in groups of twos and threes, and with some of the solutions found online [and cited], but with minor and interesting variations and with happy commentary and extra solutions and even new research. That made me really happy to see: the students had worked together, as I had hoped that they would, and they clearly enjoyed the challenges, going above and beyond to solve and produce beautiful and interesting maths. I rewarded them accordingly, with feedback praise and good marks, and told them that they were doing what real mathematical researchers do: investigate, look at what others have done, think and understand, collaborate, share ideas, be creative and inquisitive, and try to come up with creative new mathematical ideas. It’s actually hard, at student level, to avoid plagiarism in maths, since you can often only repeat old and well-known results, proofs and examples. The aim is then to show, in more subtle ways, that you have understood the material and are telling the story, so to speak, in your own words, imprinting it with your own personality, and, if possible, trying to improve it, by filling in gaps, or giving a better presentation than the standard one, or finding completely new material or explanations. This is not always easy to achieve, and this aim itself can be hard to understand for students, especially if they have been raised in cultures that emphasise rote learning and respect for authorities: Who are they to try to improve what the Masters have written? This leads me to another episode of plagiarism, perhaps the funniest but maybe also the saddest, that I have experienced. One of my students had almost written his thesis when I discovered that whole pages of his thesis had been plagiarised letter by letter from the source materials. When I pointed this out to him, he was confused, due to the cultural training that I mentioned above. He did try to understand, however, and revised a several-page proof. On reading the new version of the proof, I saw that he had replaced the variables a , b , c by x , y , z but unfortunately not consistently, so the proof was now meaningless. Poor fellow did eventually pass. A surprising number of cultural values are required and assumed in order to do maths properly, let alone deep and creative research - but they can be learned by everyone, I think.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: How do some professors give lectures without any notes/index cards at the time of the lecture?
Answer: We know the subject; we designed and created the lecture; and we prepare each time before giving it. If I prepare for a lecture and find that some detail, or the overall narrative, is a bit fuzzy to me, or if some explanation might sound fuzzy to my students, or if the emotional notes struck sound a bit off, then I think about the problem and modify what needs to be changed, until it works. Over time, most narratives, details, and conveyed emotions, become second nature to you, and you can eventually give a lecture on the fly without preparation, let alone notes.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Do professors consider themselves teachers? Why or why not?
Answer: Yes and no. My job as professor entails that I have many roles, one of which is to be a teacher. I am also a researcher, administrator, supervisor, referee/reviewer, consultant, advisor, innovator, outreach person, artist, PR person, and more. Back when I was working towards my PhD degree, I had no idea that an academic job would involve so many different roles. I naively looked forward to being a Researcher, and was dimly aware that some painful and unavoidable teaching would also be required. I definitely did not see my future career as being a teacher; in fact, I looked down on teachers, seeing them as necessary but not contributing anything new and valuable. Through years of work, however, I began to enjoy teaching more and more, and got better at it, while much of my research got harder and less enjoyable. I can’t remember the tipping point but, at some point, I realised that I enjoyed teaching more than researching. That changed my arrogant attitudes to research and teaching, and that allowed me to see that my teaching work actually contributed more - was more valuable - than my research. This has since changed once again: I have now found broader and more enjoyable and contributing fields of research, so I now enjoy my research and my teaching and even my administration work, as well as the other aspects of my work, and it all gives the satisfaction of having contributed in different ways. I now see myself as Teacher, as Researcher, as Administrator, and more. These roles often interact and support each other symbiotically, and the joys of these happy roles nicely complement each other too: it is a intense and visceral but short-lived pleasure to teach my awesome students at UNSW Sydney, whereas maths research gives a low-key and muted but very long-lasting satisfaction of achievement.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: What is it like to publish your doctoral dissertation?
Answer: At first, I was very happy. By the time that I began to write up my thesis, I had published and submitted several papers, so the writing up of the thesis was a happy and satisfying task. I had time and energy to polish the thesis and get it into a format that I really like, so it was a pleasure to get it printed and to see the final product. For the next half year, I was also happy. I had an overseas postdoc position to look forward to, and the waiting time for that felt like a holiday. I relaxed, had fun, and continued to conduct my research. Without stress to hinder me, I was very creative and productive. However, life moved on, and not long after I began my postdoc, I fell into apathy and depression. This happens to many people after they submit their PhD thesis. It is a one form of midlife crisis: for many years, perhaps most of your life, you strive towards some goals and perhaps think that life will be better or happier or easier once those goals are achieved. But life just moves on and usually just gets harder. Hardship is easy to deal with when you have purpose and meaning in your life. Goals can provide that purpose and meaning - but when you achieve those goals, then you lose that purpose and meaning, and your happiness might take a hit. What purpose does your life have once you have achieved what you strove for, for so many years? This can be a hard question to answer, and it often takes a crisis to figure out some good answers. I eventually found some answers that worked well for me, and I am now happy - but it took some time. Getting a PhD, or kids, or love, or a career, or whatever, does not make you happy, though it can give contentment and self-worth, and that can be used to create happiness. If there is a lesson to be learned here, it might be to avoid focusing too hard on specific goals but to think beyond those goals, to find deeper meaning and purpose to live by, and to enjoy the life that you have right now.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Why do some math courses not allow the use of calculators? In the real world, you would have access to a calculator, so why not learn how to do it that way?
Answer: When do you ever need to do pushups or practice piano scales? To get good at any sport or art, you need to practice lots of boring basic skills, and maths is both a sport and an art. Learning and practicing arithmetic is boring and painful to many people - but it’s a core skill needed for more interesting skills. As a bonus, arithmetic gives you a sense of numbers and proportions that is one of the most valuable real-life skills - and yet a skill that few people master well these days.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: What does it mean when a student messaged a professor a lot wanting to get to know him and then feels judged negatively?
Answer: Maybe the professor did not feel comfortable about the many messages and the intense attention. Personally, I am fine with becoming friends with students - but it is a delicate situation with significant power imbalances, sometimes both ways, which might require careful boundaries to be made, in order to protect both students and the professor. Intense attention and wanting to get to know a professor could endanger some of those boundaries. I have a few great friends among my previous students but it took a while, and some care, to let these friendships develop in a way that would not cause conflict of interest or other harm to them or to me. Did the intense attention perhaps seem obsessional or like infatuation? It can be uncomfortable and even dangerous for professors to have students crushing on them. Or maybe the professor just didn’t have time to involve himself in this interaction. Professors are really busy people, often with very little time left over for personal life. And they are usually much older than students and have other priorities in life than young people do. And, of course, getting to know people also means getting to know their flaws and weaknesses. Maybe the professor discovered some trait of the student that he found unpleasant [apart from incessant messaging], and judged accordingly.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: What is the most unbelievable/inconvenient math fact to you?
Answer: The Banach-Tarski Theorem shows how surreal the real numbers and infinity can be. It states that you can cut a 3-dimensional ball into a few parts and reassemble those parts in such a way that you now have two balls that are identical in size and volume to the one you started out with. This might seem unbelievable but it is still true. It is our wrong intuitions about volume, infinity, and “part” that cause us to be confused here. The parts here are not contiguous as they would be if we had a physical ball and a knife, and twice infinity is still just infinity, so to speak. Actually, physical matter and volume don’t exist as we intuitively think of them either: as so often, our everyday intuition limits our understanding of deeper truths. This is partly why I love the Banach-Tarski Theorem: it is surreal and demonstrates our limited understanding. I also love of this theorem because it nicely illustrates the demented genius of Banach, Tarski, and other Polish mathematicians nearly a century ago. Banach and other mathematicians would regularly meet at a trendy cafe to enjoy getting drunk and working on weird and wonderful new maths together. Their work and ideas changed mathematics and even changed our understanding of truth itself. I like to wonder how many of their ideas were due to the inspiration and creativity that drunkenness and hangovers can sometimes bring.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: How can scientific materialism explain the fact that different mathematicians approach the same situation and basically arrive at the same solution? Could it have something to do with Platonic existence?
Answer: This is an exciting question to me, since I am very interested in such philosophical questions. However, this question makes assumptions that are questionable, so a proper and in-depth answer could fill a thick tome. For a quick partial answer, I would first point that maths and technology seem to be miraculously true, verifiable and predictive, to the point that some science-philes would claim that there is nothing beyond science and that science is nothing without mathematics. Indeed, some see existence as physical, and since physics is seen as maths, and since maths is universal and therefore essentially Platonic, then existence itself is mathematical and Platonic. Funnily, others disagree, sometimes surprisingly vehemently [for otherwise mild-mannered academics], and see maths and the world as Aristotelian, or something else: there are, weirdly, a lot of politics to support and oppose all these different but ethereal philosophical stances. Personally, I have clear and simple views on these matters. First, how arrogant and, to be honest, stupid is it to assume that we are the jewel of creation, the centre of the universe and of all existence? In terms of astronomy, we have gotten a little wiser and more humble, but in terms of truth, we still see our tiny, almost infinitesimal, experience as Everything. We are literally still in the stone ages, with our highest and proudest invention being some scratches in rock [silicon-based computers], and what we know about the world around us is bugger all. To declare great conclusions about huge things like the nature of existence - and, far more arrogantly, about that which we know that we do not know - is embarrassing. Yes, we have achieved a lot in the pursuit of maths and science and technology, relative to our own tiny capabilities, but that does in no way mean that we now know everything. In fact, our very own Science tells us, the more we discover, that Existence is far weirder, far more surreal, and even far less real, than we might ever be able to imagine. That much we know, and we also know that we know very little. So, it is highly unscientific to claim, as scientific materialism does, that everything exists - which, as we know from Science, it does not - and that it is scientifically measurable and describable - which, again, we know from Science that it is not. Apart from quantum considerations, parallel universes, black matter, the question of qualia, the putative ethical measure of pain, and much more, there is so much that we simply cannot and never will be able to understand, or even encounter. The more we know, the less we know, so to speak. As for technology, Mother Nature was far better at that one billion years ago than we will ever be. Humility is in order but we are like 3-year olds, proudly waving our finger paintings around. So, scientific materialism and Platonism might be correct but probably aren’t, and we would certainly be both arrogant and stupid to conclude that they are. But then what about the magical ability of maths to be universally correct and to even let us model and predict Existence? Does this not invalidate what I’ve just written above? No: our maths is what we have [almost] all agreed on. Whenever we might disagree about some maths, we trim it until we can agree on what remains, at which point we call it Universally True, at least until someone else comes and convincingly disagrees, which regularly happens in the history of maths. Why then does Science seem to obey maths so well? Well, the Science that we have now is exactly that which is based on maths: biased. We have trimmed from Science everything outside of that which can be described by maths, leaving us just that which, from our very tiny and locally stable world-view, seems to be mathematically amenable to description and prediction. Given a slightly bigger and deeper view of things, our Science would quite likely turn out to be quite wrong, as it has so many times before. In previous times, religion and mythology and mysticism and many other frames of mind fulfilled the same sort of functions as maths in describing and predicting Existence. Maths has possibly done a better job at this but some would argue otherwise - and, more importantly, it is easy to imagine, given the evolution of frameworks, that something far better than maths might come along, to describe and predict all that which maths fails at. My guess is that we will continue to see further into the mystically realms of [sur]reality but that this will come at the cost of certainty and the notion of truth, even the notion of the our own meaningful existence. That got a bit mystical and fuzzy, haha, but this is the super-short and superficial version of what could fill books. Interesting - and humbling - stuff!

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Why are math professors so fond of chalks?
Answer: Because it is awesome! :D OK, that might require some explanation. From my point of view as lecturer and tutor, chalk on a blackboard is the best and easiest format of writing, as long as the chalk and the blackboard are of decent quality. I don’t mind writing on whiteboards but it’s harder to write nicely, and the text is harder for students to read. I’ve also tried document cameras: my handwriting is slightly better than my board work but the page is far smaller, usually too small, than my board work. Writing on iPads, Surfaces etc. is worse, apart from my reMarkable - but that nearly amounts to writing on paper. Yep: chalkboard rules, still. From the viewpoint of my many and various students, from large 1st year classes to small postgraduate classes, the consensus is clear: blackboards rule. This used to surprise me, thinking that students would prefer newer tech but they are consistently in favour of blackboards. Many university departments and faculties got rid of blackboards and, due to sharing teaching spaces, put pressure on us mathematicians and statisticians to do the same. Luckily, we resisted and our blackboards are safe for now - but it was our students and their student feedback, often and explicitly in favour of blackboard work, that gave us the support needed to protect our blackboards. New/hi tech is often great - but so is low/old tech. Tailored blends are usually best.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Do professional mathematicians ever get stuck on results that ultimately turn out to have proofs so easy they can't help but ask themselves, "how did I miss that?"
Answer: Yes; this happens frequently. Mathematical research is vicarious and unpredictable - and therefore, to me at least, exciting and adventurous. There is a large element of luck involved in conducting mathematical research, and your line of sight might be blocked from some result, if your thinking and your methods are not quite what is required in that moment. If you change your perspective just slightly, then the results might snap into focus, and then you get that “How did I miss that?” reaction. That feels nice and funny but can also be disappointing, if the result turned out to be trivial or obvious. When it comes to others’ existing research, there have been countless times when I have bashed my mind against the wall of a paragraph or even a single sentence in a proof, sometimes for days. And then, often after a change of scenery and some distraction, I see the answer clear as day: it is usually some detail that I had overlooked, or some tiny misunderstanding that led me astray. What sets professional mathematicians apart from most others, however, is that we are very stubborn and persist at some problem long after most sane people would give up. We might now and then be forced to yield on research that leads nowhere - but we usually persevere through existing proofs until the light of understanding dawns on us. Finally, there is teaching. My students often point out more elegant proofs than the ones that I thought of. That always makes me happy, partly because I am proud of them, and partly also because this causes the students and I to acts as happy collaborators, happily proposing and discussing ideas and solutions with each other.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: How could you explain the idea of mathematical proofs to a child?
Answer: A mathematical proof is just an explanation, nothing more and nothing less. Not-too-little kids understand what explanations are. Understanding does not always follow hereditary rules of logic, so we cannot conclude that kids also therefore understand the concept of explanations concerning some specific topic. It is however my experience that kids do in fact understand this notion, even if the details of particular proofs are either too boring or difficult to bother understanding. Therefore, my explanation would be as follows: “A mathematical proof of something is just an explanation of why that something is true.”.

Question: What is the best technique to attack this problem, "Recognition of handwritten mathematical expressions and its translation to LaTex"?
Answer: Handwritten maths is surprisingly hard to computer-recognise and convert to typeset mathematics, far harder than normal handwritten text. This is because maths is written in 2D, rather than in 1D, and since mathematical notation relies far more on context. It was such a hard problem that many people thought that it might take decades into the future before we could develop decent maths handwriting recognition software. It is therefore also surprising that a lot of maths-recognition breakthroughs have recently happened, and there are now many adequate maths recognition apps available. Here are several links to those apps, and there will presumably be many better ones soon to follow: What is the status of generating LaTeX from handwriting (i.e., OCR)?

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: What would you advise a student who feels he already has a higher level of critical thinking, or even IQ, than most of his professors?
Answer: I’ve taught and mentored countless students who are brighter than me, and it’s always a joy and privilege. They are often excited about topics that are of interest to me, and they often have excellent ideas and insights, so I’ve enjoyed many excellent discussions with them. Whenever possible, I invite them to do research with me, and that has sometimes led to collaboration. These students have always been polite, and although they are smarter than me, they have also always recognised that I have experience and insight that might be of use to them: being bright, having excellent critical and creative thinking, and having some great new ideas is only part of what it takes to do research and get it published. In turn, these students bring out some paternal instinct in me, and I feel like helping and supporting them to become mature, successful and happy researchers. So, my advice to her or him is usually: “Welcome, and feel free to drop by and chat/email anytime! :) ”.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: What don’t they tell you about being a professor?
Answer: That it’s hard work. There is sometimes the view that professors idly and arrogantly sit around in their ivory towers, professing to be experts, and doing little else. As a rule, however, the reality is that professors actually work far harder than others in comparable industry jobs (and for far less money). To some, completing a PhD degree is an impressive achievement - but this is little compared to completing the next step towards becoming a professor - the dreaded postdoc period. Once you survive that period, you become assistant professor and it is only then that you will learn what it means to be busy, with heaps of teaching and administrative roles on top of your research. And so on: each step up the academic ladder makes your workload bigger and your responsibilities harder. Most full professors are insanely busy. Luckily, you get stronger and wiser too, so each increase in workload and responsibility does not feel so tough, and, these days, I welcome new challenges and responsibilities. I love my job, for enough reasons to write a separate post about, and would recommend it to anyone interested in being a professor - but don’t expect that it will lead to a life of leisure.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: If I shuffle a newly opened deck of cards, lay it aside and then shuffle a second newly opened deck, what is the probability that both shuffles will be identical?
Answer: If this were a high school maths problem, then the answer would be 1 out of the number of ways in which to shuffle the second deck, which is 1/52!, or 1 52 × 51 × ⋯ × 1 = 1 80658175170943878571660636856403766975289505440883277824000000000000 . In other words, it would never happen. However, in real life, two decks from the same factory are likely to be exactly the same before shuffling. Also, it is actually extremely hard to construct anything that resembles true randomness, and it is quite hard and time-consuming to shuffle a deck of cards so that they seem randomly shuffled. In the problem at hand, your shuffling methods would usually be the same for both decks, so this would vastly increase the probability of the two shuffled decks to be identical. However, it would still depend on how you shuffle them. If your shuffling methods lead to cycles (for instance, if you simply kept swapping two half-decks), then there would only be a small number of actual shuffled deck configurations, and then the probability of the two shuffled decks being identical would be very large, perhaps even expressible in whole percentages. If on the other hand, your shuffling methods lead to long cycles or even the whole array of shuffled-deck configurations, then the probability in question would depend on how long you shuffle the second deck compared to how long you shuffled the first deck. If you were impatient, then the probability is high (perhaps a few percent) that the two decks are identical; if you are very patient and shuffled each deck for a long time, then the probability would be smaller; and if you are erratic and shuffled one deck for far longer than the other, then the probability of having identical decks would be microscopic. Of course, you could simplify the problem by not shuffling at all but just throw the cards up in the air and picking them up. That would give a far better approximation at true random shuffling, and the answer to the problem would (roughly) again be 1/52! .

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Is algebra really necessary for students who don't want to be mathematicians?
Answer: Yes: William Mealey’s excellent reply below explains why. No: In reality, most school maths is taught badly, often by under-supported and overburdened teachers, many of whom are filling in and don’t know or like maths, and who must adhere to the confines of badly designed curriculae whose immediate aim it is to get you to pass some test. This sort of learning does not train your brain muscles or deepen your understanding. It is a painful waste of time and resources, and it makes many students hate maths and mathematical thinking. That is a real shame, especially when good education could let so many more students love maths and benefit greatly.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: If humans didn't have to "work" for a living and robots managed all of the labor, how different would our society become and how would people find "meaning" in their life?
Answer: This has already happened. For thousands of years, ruling classes in various cultures have found “robots” to do all the work. This gave the ruling classes the problem of boredom, which could be partly solved by entertainment or taking up some industrious hobby. A lot of art and science has resulted from bored noblemen and -women, as well as bored vicars and others with religious leisure. Entertainment does not provide good purpose and meaning but industrious hobbies can. Today, most of us who live in the richer societies of the world are also members of the leisure classes, even though we don’t know it and certainly don’t feel like it. We live better than most kings of old, with luxuries that those old kings never could imagine, and most of our jobs are completely unnecessary, ficticious and replaceable: we work in order to serve the role of consumers, to have social status, and to have purpose and meaning. However, this is an expensive fiction for our societies to upkeep, and the faint rumblings of change can already be heard, with talk of universal basic income being discussed here and there, and tested out in the progressive vanguards of the West. Once most of the more vacuous and superfluous jobs become financially untenable at the 40-hours/week-for-everyone level that we have been used to, we will face more boredom and loss of purpose. Boredom is easy to take care of: we already have entertainment; it is our biggest industry these days. Purpose is harder to come by. In Scandinavia and a few other places around the world, the social infrastructure to provide purpose and meaning in non-work life has been established over the last thirty years. There, people already define themselves in terms that do not necessarily involve work but which are more personal and social. In those parts of the world, jobs might give way to other pursuits that pay off in social status rather than in money. In the rest of the world, there is no social infrastructure for a life of leisure; in most places, it is still taboo to think of living comfortably without a job. There, losing a job is to become unemployed. Given the past decades in the US, we can see how this can happen in incremental degrees: jobs lose their value and workers slowly lose their wages and need to work longer and harder, perhaps even taking up more jobs to get by. Robots are more expensive than cheap labour, and much more expensive than slave-like labour of prison populations, undocumented immigrants, and the captured poor. This is the dystopian contrast to the brighter future that Scandinavia is starting to show. Between these contrasts might lie most of the world, in some not-distant future. My guess is that universal basic incomes will replace (expensive and unproductive) jobs in order to cut overall societal costs - but that the stigma against receiving public money for free will mean that new fictitious jobs will be created in order for those receiving the universal income to “work”, only for somewhat less than we are used to being paid for our present “jobs”. Combined perhaps with fewer work hours per week, and a slow shift towards a softening of stigmas, the “work” might change in character too, for instance towards jobs that would at present be called hobbies. There are more factors to throw in the mix here too, including the increasingly abstract and mathematical nature of skilled jobs, the quickly emerging machine-learning “robot” takeover of services and research, and many other factors. A brave new world!

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: What should I do, my son and daughter teamed up on me and ditched school now they are upstairs playing video games?
Answer: Change the wifi password and withhold their weekly allowance. During school hours, loudly play music that you like and they hate. If that doesn’t send them out of the house and to school, then keep serving them kale for dinner. Or just join them upstairs for a game.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: How does it feel to be good at math?
Answer: It feels good, for different reasons. I love being good at maths because this lets me enjoy lots of fascinating, beautiful and challenging maths, and because it has given me an awesome job as teacher and researcher. It also lets me see the world in ways that give insight and awe, perhaps in similar ways to how mystics, philosophers or artists might see the world, and I love these “third eye” insights. I am very grateful for all this that maths has given me. It also feels good to see others be good at maths. It’s always awesome to see a student achieve that Aha! moment, after a hard struggle with some maths. It also feels good to collaborate with a colleague on some interesting maths research, or to enjoy seeing a colleague find some big and beautiful mathematical result. Or see students and amateur mathematicians enjoy maths and sometimes discover beautiful maths that us professional mathematicians could not see. And maths can feel good even if you are not good at maths. Most school maths is taught badly and is scary, boring, and test-focused. It doesn’t have to be that way though, and I hope that this changes so that more people can enjoy maths, whether they are good at it or not.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Are mathematicians generally poorly paid, given that the prize money for the Fields medal which is the most prestigious award for mathematicians is insultingly small at CAD 15,000?
Answer: Imagine winning an Olympic medal. The prize money, if any, is not important, only the achievement. Winning a Fields medal is an even greater achievement, and the prize money means even less. Are mathematicians generally poorly paid? No: we are paid well. As an academic mathematician, I get paid roughly 2–3 the median national salary here in Australia (135k vs. 55k or 44k, depending on how you measure the median), which sometimes feels embarrassing and even shameful but is probably fair since my workload is also roughly 2–3 times as large as that of average white-collar jobs. On the other hand, I could earn 2–3 times more by choosing a job as industry mathematician in data science or finance, so some might see my salary as small. I love my job though and don’t want to change career. To return to the question at hand, is there an correlation, as implied, between the “insultingly small” prize money for the Fields medal and the salaries of mathematicians? One might suspect a correlation, since some mathematicians display proud and even arrogant streaks of asceticism and anti-materialism. Together with a tradition for humour, this explains small prize amounts of $1000 or less, even $10 or $1, that Paul Erdős and other famous mathematicians have promised as awards for solving particular mathematical problems. As it turns out, this does not impact salaries of mathematicians. Those salaries are determined by academic and industrial enterprise agreements and by job market supply and demand. And any lingering correlation suspicion might evaporate entirely when you think of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, awarding you US$1M if you solve any of them, and the ~US$700K bonus that accompanies the Abel Award - which some see as even more prestigious than the Fields medal.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Do college professors care about students with headphones in during lecture (or playing Tetris on a laptop) if it's boring to them?
Answer: Yes; I do. Because that means that I have failed as a teacher. My job (and privilege and joy) is to make each lecture and tutorial a happy and collective experience for everyone attending, including me, for us all together to understand, appreciate and enjoy (and hopefully create) some beautiful mathematics. This not only means presenting the mathematics clearly and dynamically. It means also to engineer the mood of the classroom to become happy and collaborative, inviting questions, new ideas and discussions. It’s a happy thing when you can get hundreds of people to forget that they are 1st year students, that the auditorium is big and scary, and the maths even scarier. And it’s a beautiful thing when this leads to the happy and excited vibe of friends gathering to discover and explore more together. So, I don’t mind at all if someone is sleeping in my lectures, or is doing other work, or if they come and go (quietly) during the lecture, or even have their headphones on and are socialising, gaming, streaming or whatever. I do mind, though, if this is because I failed to include and engage them, and I do mind if this failure and opting-out is disruptive and might infect others. To be honest, I can’t remember the last time that any disruptive sort of mis-vibe happened in my lectures; it’s rare and long ago. Treat people with respect, and they will live up to your expectations. Care about them, and they will care about you: happy feedback loops.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: What do mathematicians and statisticians just "get" that other people don't?
Answer: Truth. Most people can be persuaded by fake news, marketing misinformation, political spin, random memes, conspiracy theories, common “knowledge”, and fear. Mathematicians and statisticians are less easily led astray. As a mathematician, I’m trained, like my statistician colleagues, to independently and critically assess information, rather than just accept what I am told. I am also thoroughly trained at abstract thinking, at visualising ideas, and at creating new information myself, based on whatever basic information is available. Perhaps most importantly, we are trained to have an excellent sense of proportion. This means that you can’t easily fool us, and we see through most of the torrent of lies and errors in news, advertisements, politics and elsewhere (which can be frustrating to both us and to everyone around us). We won’t be scared of “terrorist attacks” or dying in a plane crash, because these things never actually happen to anyone, from a statistical point of view. It also means that we often see interesting and even beautiful details and structure in the world around us that is clear for everyone to see if only they knew how to see it. We mathematicians can often be society’s visionaries but of a mostly useless sort: our visions are usually too abstract or paradigm-breaking for others to understand and accept. Unfortunately, this doesn’t make us mathematicians and statisticians overall wiser or clear-seeing than others. Others, like computer scientists, engineers and other scientists are often good at seeing things clearly like we do, and every sort of training, scientific or otherwise, gives special insight that others might not have. In fact, being able to see some truths more clearly can make you blind to other truths, like wearing one set of glasses instead of another. For instance, we mathematicians and statisticians can often be blind to cultural and emotional truths. When I was young, I often got annoyed at fashion and other group-mind culture, because they were irrational and sometimes even downright stupid. It took me a while to see that logic and factual truth sometimes weren’t important; sometimes social interactions and dynamics, and of course emotions, are far more important. And, sometimes, lies are good. As a mathematician, logic and that sense of proportion tells me that life is hard and full of future hardships and pains - but here it is healthier to be the ignorant idiot and pretend that life will overall be happy. And luckily, the quirks of our psychology make it so: memory is painted rosy, and optimism and a positive outlook paints our present and future rosy too. I sometimes wonder: my love of thinking, discovering, and creating new ideas and insights has probably made me wiser in many ways than most. But has this also made me less wise than most? Seeing further than others can segregate and alienate you from others; it can blind you to other truths; and it might not be the best path to happiness and contentment. What is wisest: being wise or being ignorant?

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Why are we forced to learn algebra when most average people don't use this on a day to day basis unless you're specializing in a certain job?
Answer: It’s like learning to run or do pushups: most average people don’t use these skills on a day to day basis but training them makes us stronger and smarter, and gives us some very basic and transferable life skills.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Why is the 1998 Danish film The Idiots considered one the 1000 best films?
Answer: Because it is a fantastic film. That doesn’t make it an easy film to watch. The director, Lars von Trier, loves to tease and torture his audiences with uncomfortable emotions and existential questions, and this is particularly evident in this film. As viewers, we can identity with many of the characters in the film, and we recognise many of their flaws as our own. The questions and truths of the film make it clear just how hypocritical and restrictive normal society can be - but also that rebellious counter-cultures in search of truth, honesty, and freedom so often become more hypocritical and restrictive than the societies that they oppose. As in many of his other films, Lars von Trier acknowledges here that his own criticisms are themselves open to criticism, and the film is deliberately allowed to fall into absurdity and unscripted chaos. With resignation, pain and humour, von Trier seems be saying that life is what it is, and gritty reality is truer than socio-philosophical discourses. To help make the film true and honest in this realist sense, the actors and actresses were asked to live together in one house before the filming, playing and becoming their roles, and creating a tight web of intricate relationships amongst each other. This gives the film a raw and textured documentary flavour; indeed, the film intercuts retrospective interviews with the actors and actresses, asking them about their experiences with this project, and it is hard to tell whether they are commenting as their characters or as themselves; it seems that most are commenting on both at the same time. The Idiots is arguably also the most successfully created Dogma 95 film. Dogma 95 was a strongly purist and provocative declaration, by Lars von Trier, Thomas Vinterberg and two fellow filmmakers, against expensive and flashy but empty and irrelevant big-screen movies. What seemed like an arrogant and ignorable arthouse tantrum was vindicated when the first Dogma 95 film came out and won half the worlds’ film awards: the amazing and endlessly re-watchable Festen by Vintergberg. This success helped to promote the second Dogma 95 film: von Trier’s The Idiots. Like Festen, The Idiots was a masterpiece and gained additional acclaim for being a Dogma 95 film. However, whereas Festen was (and is) confronting but eminently entertaining, with beautifully sculpted script, The Idiots did not aim to entertain or have a neat script; it aims for raw emotional and existential reality. It was not made for a general audience, or at least not for their pleasure; it was made to follow the Dogma 95 rules and to serve as an honest, free and provocative - and yet also self-doubting and soul-searching - proclamation/discussion, from Lars von Trier to the world and also to the himself. The Idiots is not an easy film to watch but I highly recommend watching it anyway!

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: You've spent your youth learning a trade, but there is limited demand so the only job you can get is teaching others. Why is this not terribly shameful?
Answer: If you had set your goals on another career, and had to “make do” with teaching, then that might feel terribly shameful at the time. A cure for that shame is to be the best damned teacher that you can be. My high school maths teacher, the amazing Ivan Tafteberg, was such a teacher. On finishing his maths PhD, he found himself in a downturned job market and had to take a teaching job. For the next four decades, he was one of the best teachers whom I’ve had ever met. In addition to teaching, he organised outreach events by university professors for high school students; he wrote many excellent maths books for teachers and students; and he even conducted and published mathematical and historical research. Years after I left high school, I met Ivan by chance and started to keep sporadic contact with him. He, on the other hand, had kept himself updated on my academic progress and on that of other former students, through the grapevine of colleagues and some of those former students. So when I eventually completed my own maths PhD, I was happy but not quite surprised to see Ivan attend my thesis defense. I was however very surprised that he gave me as present an 1888 edition of a book by Julius Petersen, one of the founders of the topic of my thesis (graph and matroid theory). The previous owner was Sven Bundgaard, the founder of my university maths department. Ivan had found it some years prior in an antique bookshop and had thought of me, and had waited until my graduation to give it to me. What a perfect, thoughtful, and lovely present! Unlike Ivan, I was lucky to get the sort of job that I had been aiming for, and I am now a university mathematician. I enjoy my maths research but I also love teaching. Ivan’s exemplary teaching and his dedication to do good beyond the classroom inspires me still today, as I try to become a better teacher and better person. Thank you, Ivan!

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: My advisor never took me to a conference. Is that bad for my future career?
Answer: Conferences are very useful for promoting yourself and your work, for creating new connections and collaborations, and for getting new ideas and motivation. So yes; it is a very good idea to go to conferences, especially if you are a student. Are you still studying, and can you get access to travel funds? If so, then you could always go to a conference on your own; you don’t need your supervisor to take you. However, don’t worry much about not going to a conference! Your career relies mostly on your research output, and you can promote yourself in other ways than via conferences. You could, for instance, email professors that you would like impress, and send them your best work. That will make them notice you, and if you’re lucky, then this might even result in fruitful collaboration. Best of luck!

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: How did you choose your career? Did you regret your choice?
Answer: By being drunk, young and arrogant. It was at my first big university party, and I had gotten too drunk too quickly. I don’t remember much from that evening but one memory still burns clearly with shame. I was bragging to two of my student mentors that I would do a maths PhD. With great patience and kindness, they tried to explain to me how hard it would be to even get considered for the PhD program. As a fresh 1st year student, they gently hinted, I had no clue about the work and dedication involved, nor whether I would even be interested in pursuing a PhD, once a few years of undergraduate studies had passed. The next day, I woke up with a bad hangover and with even worse shame at this flashback. But, sometimes, you can get Nemesis to forgive you. I spent the next four years of undergraduate studies on working hard to get great grades so that I could fulfill my own prophecy, and whenever my motivation dropped, that shameful memory gave me renewed energy. In the end, I did complete my PhD and had by then found healthier motivation to do well and to work hard: combinatorics, the area of my research, is awesomely fun and challenging, and I love this maths still today. So, I thank the drunk, young and arrogant me, and I do not even slightly regret the choice he made for me.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: What mathematics concept is the most important to grasp as a daily life skill?
Answer: A basic sense of size. It is amazing how useful even just a little sense of size, proportion, and likelihood can be. And it is alarming how little of this sense most people have. Without this sense, you are at risk of being persuaded by a torrent of lies and exaggerations from ads, marketing, politicians, and others intent on manipulating you. With this sense, however, and ideally some basic skill in arithmetic and logic, you have the tools to quickly check whether the claims made to you are believable, dubious or completely outrageous. You will be able to better see through spin, false news, and memed myths. You will also be much better protected against financial risks, including wasteful spending, poor savings, gambling, and dodgy investments that your bank advisor or real estate agents might suggest. Gambling probabilities are almost never in your favour but it takes that sense of proportion and likelihood to see this clearly. I started to write a list of examples of using this sense in daily life but the list quickly grew huge. Instead, it might be more interesting and fun for you to look for and notice the many times that you estimate, compare or evaluate something. We use our sense of size all day and every day.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: If you could go back in time and delete one invention, what would it be?
Answer: Time travel, for fun paradox ;) A more serious reply would be life’s invention of self-cannabalising. It’s efficient and without it, life might not be able to exist, but it has caused a billion years of untold pain (alongside all other beautiful qualia).

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Is it ok to ask for a recommendation letter from a professor I haven't talked to in two years?
Answer: Yes, definitely. I often get asked for letters of recommendation by students years after I have taught them. It doesn’t hurt to ask. On the other hand, the professor might have trouble immediately remembering who you are. It is therefore a good idea to send them your grades/CV and remind them, with details, of who you are and how they knew you. Giving clear and useful information will help the professor to write a clear and useful letter of recommendation.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: To be a mathematician, do you have to be good in all math or just the field of math you want to go into?
Answer: You can be a top mathematician and yet only know very little outside of your areas of expertise. In fact, maths is too huge and sprawling for anyone to understand and master all of its areas. As a useful rule of thumb, it is good to be both deep and broad in your mathematical knowledge and skills: going deeply into certain areas of expertise makes you a better expert, and broadly exploring other areas of maths gives you better general overview. It is sometimes hard to balance both the depth and the breadth of your mathematical research but both are important. However, being good at maths is not enough to make you a good mathematician. You also need other qualities, like being able to search out and identify potential sources of quality research, being able to create new research, and being able to induce, visualise and manipulate abstract concepts. You also need creativity, intuition, inquisitiveness, independence, clarity of thought, tenacity, inner drive, courage, patience, collaborative skills, humility, generosity, diplomacy, tough skin, attention to detail, problem-solving skills, pattern recognition skills, … and much more. Personally, I’m good at a lot of combinatorics and other areas of discrete maths, and I’m good at thinking creatively, intuitively and abstractly, and I’m independent, inquisitive and tenacious. On the other hand, I’m know very little maths outside of discrete maths, haven’t done any calculus for two decades, and really suck at topology and abstract higher algebra. Luckily, I’ve rarely had any need to be good at those areas in my research. However, I’m also mercurial, undisciplined, and sometimes slow and dull. I can’t always rely on flashes of creative insight and abstract association: sometimes, you just have to sit down and look at the hard and tiny details of the problem at hand. I’m pretty bad at that. Happily, there is often a solution for this: collaboration. If a colleague in my area is not so creative but is very good at disciplined and detailed-oriented problem-solving, then they and I can help each other by pooling our complementary skill sets, and together get some good and happy research done. Maths does not need to be a solitary game! ^_^

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: What is a form of math we use everyday without knowing it?
Answer: You use maths every second of every day. You use maths when you listen and when you laugh. You use maths when you make someone else laugh. You use maths when you get together with someone and you use maths when you break up with them. You’re using maths to read this right now. Our acts and thoughts and even our emotions are all, to some extent, mathematical. The maths involved is as old as life itself, and includes signal processing (e.g., hearing and sight), pattern recognition (e.g., text reading and attraction+compatibility), measuring entropy/randomness (e.g., laughter and humour), game theory (e.g., getting together with someone), optimisation (e.g., choosing to break up with someone), and countless others forms of maths. In fact, I predict that many yet-unknown forms of maths lie in wait for us to discover through the study of our own individual and collective behaviours, thoughts, and emotions.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: How often does your job require you to use Algebra or a higher level math?
Answer: All the time! But I’m a university research mathematician and might not be all that representative ;)

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Should you apologize for sending an email to a professor after midnight?
Answer: No; certainly not. Professors receive - and often check - emails around the clock, from all over the world: academic work is an international pursuit. Given how busy professors are, they are used to managing time and tasks, so don’t necessarily expect an immediate reply. But the positive flip side to that coin is that you don’t need to worry about sending emails to professors outside of what in other professions would be considered normal work hours.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Should I drop from a Ph.D. program if none of the faculty members is interested in working with me?
Answer: No. I was in that situation myself. Having done well in my undergraduate studies, I was keen to study for a PhD degree, so I asked my favourite lecturer whether he would be interested in supervising me. He declined, being too busy with his firm as side-business to his academic position. I therefore asked him whether he would agree to be my official supervisor, signing paperwork now and then but not doing any actual supervision. Luckily, he agreed. I then asked him how to find some professor to supervise me, and he told me to use Google. And that, it turned out, was the best advice that he could have given me. Knowing nothing about supervisors, I googled to find the best researchers at the best universities in my field of research (combinatorics and graph theory), and I quickly found several top researchers to ask for informal supervision. Most replied favourably (I’ve found that most top researchers in combinatorics are lovely and generous people), so I chose one of them, Prof. Gian-Carlo Rota. For the first year of my PhD, I visited Prof. Rota and his other students and colleagues at M.I.T., and there learned and worked far better and harder than I ever would have at my home university under some mediocre supervisor. Sadly Prof. Rota died near the end of that year, and I returned home. Another brilliant researcher, Prof. Peter Cameron, very kindly agreed to continue my supervision, with a slightly different thesis direction. Over the next three years, I visited him and his active combinatorics group several times, at what was then called Queen Mary, University of London, including for two half-year visits. Prof. Cameron provided me with top-rate feedback and encouragement, and, as at M.I.T., I was once again highly productive and creative in my work. The networking and stimulation in these environments was invaluable as well. Today, I am very grateful for being turned down by my lecturer: it directed me to a tougher but far better and happier path of research and learning. It would have been nice to have had a supporting local supervisor, maybe even a productive research group to belong to (most of my early papers were sole-authored). But then I would not have been blessed by the opportunities that my unofficial supervisions by Prof. Rota and Prof. Cameron provided me with, and I would not have had the same opportunities to grow as independent researcher. So, if you are part of a PhD program and can’t find a good local supervisor but can find funding to travel, then I strongly recommend that you contact top researchers elsewhere for their informal supervision. Good luck!

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: My girlfriend is mad that I won’t buy her a car with my savings, I have tried to explain to her it’s my money but she’s threatening to leave me, how do I fix this problem?
Answer: Buy her a cool LEGO toy car. That way, you’ll get to have fun building it when she leaves you. Which she will anyway. And good riddance.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Can you explain what you use your PhD for in simple language?
