Answer: The answer depends on which numbers we here are dealing with. If these are real numbers, then √ is a well-defined function on all non-negative numbers: if x ≥ 0 , then √ x is the usual square root of x . Actually, we could also have defined there to be two square roots, √ x and − √ x , since they both have x as their square: ( √ x ) 2 = x and ( − √ x ) 2 = x . However, we prefer to keep things simple here and just choose the non-negative - and largest - of these two numbers to be our official square root. Therefore, in this case, √ ( − 5 ) 2 = √ 25 = 5 . However, if we look at other numbers than the real numbers, such as the complex numbers, then it is a little more complicated. Just like for positive real numbers, each non-zero complex number z has two numbers α and β that can be seen as square roots of z : α 2 = z and β 2 = z . However, unlike for the real numbers, we have no way to choose just one of these to be the official square root, since there is no natural way in which to strictly order complex numbers by how large they are. For instance, there is no most natural way to determine which of the four complex numbers 1 , i , − 1 , − i is largest. Therefore, the notation √ does not make sense as a well-defined function on complex numbers. That is, however, only true if you insist on √ being a number. If you don’t insist on that, then we could instead let √ z be the set of roots { α , β } of z .  That is messy and not as simple as a single positive number, as in the real case, but it does provide us with a well-defined function giving the roots of square numbers. In this case, the square root of ( − 5 ) 2 would be √ ( − 5 ) 2 = √ 25 = { − 5 , 5 } . There is no generally agreed-upon standard for dealing with √ when it comes to complex numbers and other more complicated types of numbers; you are free to choose your own [well-defined] definitions!

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: How common is it for researchers in mathematics to have 1000 citations or more?
Answer: Quite common. I have nearly 800 citations and am about halfway through my paid academic career. Citation counts tend to grow accumulatively rather than linearly, so I expect to get 2000–3000 citations before I retire from research. My fellow pure mathematicians have, on rough average, the same order of citations. Applied mathematicians and statisticians have many more citations than us. These citation numbers in pure maths are very low compared to other science disciplines. This is mainly due to two reasons. The first reason is that pure maths is a slow and deep [but rewarding] discipline, so it takes us longer to produce results than in other disciplines. Indeed, our average publication rate is so slow that it has been used as baseline for comparing publication rates in other scientific disciplines. The second reason is cultural and stylistic: in pure maths, we like to get to the point quickly, without preamble or extended discussion. In contrast, articles in most other scientific disciplines include long introductions and discussions. These include large numbers of citations, of the authors’ own previous work, of their colleagues’ work, and of the historically relevant work in the particular field. That gives high citation rates, compared to our citation rates in pure maths. The disparity between rates of citations in pure maths and in other scientific disciplines used to handicap us pure mathematicians when applying for grants and jobs. Luckily, these disparities are now taken into account, and our research output is now usually measured relative to discipline-specific metrics.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Is there a way to study math when you have trouble retaining basic information relating to math?
Answer: Maths is a sprawling subject and learning to master it is a bit like learning a language, sport, music or art: there are some basics to learn, and then there’s lots of practice. With a little effort and patience, you will begin to get the hang of maths, and once you have a feeling for some maths, then you can go on to do more challenging and instructive maths. At that point, try to understand what you are doing: to be a good mathematician, you mostly need understanding, intutition/visualisation, creativity, curiosity, and persistance. You can train all of these as well. Also, like in those other disciplines, it really helps you learn if you’re having fun. So, one way to learn effectively would be to go have fun and challenge your maths-learning brain with the problems at Brilliant or at Project Euler (more coding-focused), for instance, where you can also see other users’ answers and quickly pick up a lot of understanding and tips.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: How true is it that everyone is either a math or an English person, but never both? Why?
Answer: No; you can be good at both. There are several reasons for why maths and language skills are seen to be mutually exclusive. One reason is that school subjects and classes get easier to administrate if you divide subjects into big and clunky categories, like Art, Science, Humanities or whatever. That is useful but makes it harder for students to choose subjects freely and broadly, and it gives the wrong impression that these categories are segregated. Another reason is cultural: these days, Western culture often sees maths and STEM subjects as [unpopularly/trendy] nerdy, rational, logical, “linear thinking”, and in contrast to the [popularly/trendy] “human”, “creative”, “emotional”, “social” subjects, which language is seen to below to. This cultural view is wrong: maths is also creative and emotional, and language is also rule-bound - but you might not get to do much creative and happy maths in school; that often comes later, partly due to bad curricula and teachers, and overemphasis on assessments. In other cultures and in the past, maths and language were seen as far more overlapping than they are in the West today: think of classical Greek poetry and its strict mathematical patterns, for instance.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: How is math different than language if it can be used to explain or justify almost anything?
Answer: What is a language? We could answer that it is a method of expressing information, with some sort of agreed-upon elements and rules. That leads to more questions, like “What is information?”, “What are the elements and rules, and how precisely do we need to define them?”, “What does ‘express’ mean?”, “Is there a role of ‘listener’ here, and if so, then are the roles of the ‘speaker’ and ‘listener’ separate?”, “What is the purpose, if any, of this language?” and many more. These questions might seem overly philosophical, turning a simple concept - language - into a mess of confused concepts. However, we do actually need to think about these questions in order to understand and be good at everyday life, like clear communication, relationships, empathy, art, technology, and much more. Think of a good film or a pretty painting: they have quality because those many of those philosophical questions have been answered well: What is the story or emotion [information] to be told? What is the format of the story-telling? Who is the audience and how can the audience be engaged in dialogue? And so on. Or think of language recognition software. In the 1960s, computer scientists allied themselves with psychologists in order to model human [written] language by computer programs. They looked at words [elements] and tried to express language in mathematical ways, following logical rules of spelling, semantics, grammar and so on. They failed spectacularly but, in doing so, they showed just how complex our human languages and thinking really are. Even today, more than half a century later, we don’t even have good enough approximate understanding of human language and thinking to develop good voice-recognition software or even decent text-recognition software. Ironically, mathematical text, which you would suppose to be logical and easier than most other text, is far harder to text-recognise than usual text, partly because it must be interpreted in 2D rather than in 1D, but also, perhaps surprisingly, because it usually assumes far more unwritten context than does usual text. To see how the language of maths is different from our usual human written or verbal languages, we can look at those philosophical questions again: What is information? Maths: Countless abstract concepts and their relationships. The concepts are only included if they can be defined in ways that appear to yield no contradictions, and they only make sense and have value when placed in specific contexts of other concepts. On the other hand, a mathematical concept or relationship between concepts [i.e., a mathematical ‘truth’] is only promoted if we find it beautiful or useful. The rules are chosen to be mathematically logical: there are several variations of these logics but none of them allow logical contradiction, and most of them serve to infer new conceptual developments and relationships from previous concepts and relationships. Human language: Most concepts are taken from our human experience and from the ever-evolving cultures, big and small, that give both the concepts, our experience, and indeed ourselves context and meaning. We can and do talk about philosophical and even mathematical truths, but you would be a poor teacher if you were to try to teach maths strictly in the language of maths: we are more comfortable with what we can experience, even if it is just a mental image or sensation of a concept. Our concepts are usual fluidly defined, usually by association, not strictly or with mathematical logic: we struggle with formal definitions. The rules of language are much more fluid that those of mathematics, at granular level following semi-strict spelling or grammatical rules but mostly adhering to context and association, and even those granular rules bend and break and become new rules. The main logical formats inherent in these rules are by association and by present social and linguistic norms, and those keeping changing. What is being expressed, by whom and to whom it is expressed, and why? Maths: There are several purposes for expressing maths. Someone might want to use maths to build or test something or to pass some exam or win some maths competition. Here, the information is usually a collection of calculated numbers or a line of mathematical reasoning [proof], and it is expressed usually by one person or a small group of people, either to themselves or to another audience, and the communication is mostly one-way, no dialogue. The numbers themselves, and the proud fact that they were calculated by the person/people expressing them, is the information itself; the expression is [mostly] also the message. A similar purpose for expressing maths is to analyse data in order to be able to present numbers that might influence the opinions of others about some non-maths issue. Here, again, the communication is one-way, from the mathematician [here including statisticians] to a broader but still usually passive audience. Maths is sometimes also expressed for its aesthetic properties, a form of abstract art that can be enjoyed like other art forms: here, the purpose is not to transmit a message or to influence opinions but to convey beauty and emotion. However, the communication is still usually one-way, from the ‘artist’ to the appreciative audience. More interestingly, a major mode of mathematical expression when mathematicians [amateur or professional] conduct research and problem-solving [e.g., Brilliant.org] together, with an interesting mix of individual effort and collaboration. Here, the purpose of mathematical expression is to show off one’s discoveries and talents, to share the joys of doing that, and to enjoy and learn from each other’s results and methods. This mix of collaboration and competition is constructive in the sense that consensus is sought, rather than division: results and methods are accepted only if they are seen as true by the majority of those with social authority among the participants involved. Mathematically speaking, mathematical expression is only seen as valuable if it lies in the intersection of the participants’ views, and those views adapt and change to align with other’s views too. This is highly consensual, far more than most other human interaction. Human language: While there might be several purposes for expressing maths, there are countless purposes for expressions using human language. In fact, the majority of expressions using our human language do not even serve to convey specific information. In terms of written English, the information rate alone is roughly 68%, meaning that the spelling and grammar itself is very sparse in actual information, with text filling roughly 3 times more than transmission of the words actually require - and this is just the words themselves, not the meaning behind them. [This bloating of text does however have a very important function: it provide excellent error-correction, so that we can quickly understand language even if there are spelling mistakes or dialectal variations or a noisy and crowded space.] We mostly communicate in order to create and to feel mutual connection, in order to share our emotions and experiences, and to create belonging and social cohesion - or, for instance, to gain social advantages or even dominance. Here, mathematical logic and ‘truth’ is of very little value; the logical formats here are association and social norms, and when consensus is sought, it is usually social consensus, often at the expense of consensus of individual truths. This is a vast and vastly intricate mode of communication, and the roles of ‘speakers’ and ‘listeners’ are fuzzy and often indistinguishable. Human language is used for many other things too, including to express mathematics and mathematical concepts and relations, but, on balance, the form and purposes are very different between these two types of languages.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: How was Paul Erdős important to the study of combinatorics?
Answer: Paul Erdős was hugely important to the development of combinatorics. He was one of the most prolific mathematical researchers in history and contributed countless important new mathematical results, methods and ideas. However, his far more important contribution to combinatorics was that he super-charged the development and acceptance of this field, and he cultivated and grew a large and happy combinatorial community. His love of the combinatorics was infectous and he promoted it through clear and elegant expositions, sometimes of old and overlooked results and theory, such as Ramsey Theory, to name just one example. Ramsey theory is now a large and thriving area of research, difficult but much beloved, but was not given deserved attention when Frank P. Ramsey published his seminal paper in 1930. His results were elegant and clearly presented but also abstract, and they were represented as results of logic more than of mathematics. Generally speaking, his results show how, in very specific context, structure and order will always prevail under any random circumstances. More specifically, we can look at some dots and draw lines between each pair of dots: this is called a complete graph. A simple case of Ramsey’s discoveries invites you to colour the lines of a complete graph in whichever way you like with a fixed number of colours. Then, as long as you have enough dots, there will always be some collection of these dots, of whichever fixed size you like, whose connecting lines are all of the same colour. Here, the important caveat is that we cannot choose that colour from the outset - but a monochromatic complete sub-graph will exist, regardless of how randomly you try to colour the lines. It might have taken many years for people to realise the value of this theory, were it not for Paul Erdős and George Szekeres who brought Ramsey’s mathematics to public attention in an 1935 article. In that article, they show-cased what is now called Ramsey’s Theorem, by [re-proving it and] applying it to provide a strikingly elegant and accessible mathematical theorem, namely an extension suggested by Esther Klein of her own result: draw dots in the plane in any way that you choose, as long as you don’t draw any three of them on a same line. Then, as long as you have enough dots, you can always find a collection of dots, of whichever fixed size you like, that form a convex polygon. Klein was given clear acknowledgement of her earlier result and her suggestion but she really ought to have been co-author on this 1935 article. She seems not to have borne grudge: two years later, she and Szekeres were married and lived happily together for nearly 70 more years. Erdős and Szekeres also proved this result by a different method, by first proving another elegant combinatorial theorem: given a sequence of n 2 + 1 different numbers, you can find at least n + 1 of the numbers which form an increasing subsequence or you can find at least n + 1 of the numbers which form a decreasing subsequence (here, the numbers in the subsequences need not be consecutive). These elegant results are very appealing and easy to understand, so many mathematicians were drawn to the study of Ramsey theory and of the sort of combinatorial results that were here displayed. That was typical of Erdős’ work: through simple and elegant articles, results and lectures, he inspired and made others excited to work in areas of combinatorics. Erdős also worked tirelessly at collaboration, visiting countless mathematicians to work with them or, often, to get them to work for him, by posing remarkably intuitive and prophetic conjectures and questions of combinatorics that would inspire others to work hard and deeply. His published papers were written in collaboration with 511 other mathematicians. That is a huge number of collaborators and explains, alongside his fame, why mathematicians invented the Erdős number that indicates the co-author distance from Erdős to any published researcher. Erdős’ spent most his time dedicated to promote and develop not only combinatorics but also the combinatorial research community. He also encouraged and helped children to study combinatorics, and he supported national schemes of providing school students with combinatorial problems and competitions. In his later years, his fame and eccentricities served to promote not only combinatorics but also mathematics as a whole. I therefore see his legacy as more than his mathematical work, though that itself was extraordinary: his real legacy is that he transformed a small and dismissed field of research and helped develop it into one of the most actively thriving and exciting fields of mathematical study today. As a combinatorial researcher myself, I am indebted to him and other pioneers of the field, who through their love and passion of combinatorics grew this field and its community. They showed how this mathematics was unifying, elegant and important but also that mathematics could also just be about solving problems and exploring ideas for the fun of it.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: What is least practically useful mathematical area of study?
Answer: I love this question and have three different perspective to offer: Perspective I: Numeracy To most people, most maths appears to be useless, and school students often ask what maths is good for when having to learn it. We certainly need numeracy, like basic arithmetic and fractions, say, in order to get along well in life, just like we need to be able to read and write. However, the rest of maths learned in school is, to be honest, mostly useless. If you were to ask a random person on the street whether they had recently calculated some calculus or solved an equation or even used Pythagoras’ Theorem, then they would almost certainly say no [and think you weird for asking the question]. The reason that this school maths is useless is that it is mostly rote learned and presented with tests in mind. Remembering a formula has next to no value unless you understand why the formula has its particular form. It is the understanding that has value, and the training in becoming better at abstract visualisation, creativity, analysis and problem solving, and independent thinking. In order to aquire these skills, you need exposure to “useless” maths which, if taught with understanding and independent thinking in mind, can train your mind. In this way, most maths can become very useful. This is true in the same way as in sports, art, music and many other disciplines: pushups or even running, say, are useless activities to learn for their own sake, just like calculating fractions and solving equations - but they are very valuable for training you to become better at things more generally. Perspective II: Mathematics seen from afar If we look at particular mathematical areas, you could be tempted to point out many that appear to be obviously without any practical use. In fact, most areas of mathematics appear to be without use, and the pure mathematician G.K. Hardy was even proud of this, bragging in 1940 that ‘I have never done anything "useful". No discovery of mine has made, or is likely to make, directly or indirectly, for good or ill, the least difference to the amenity of the world.’ The irony here is that Hardy’s beautifully useless maths is now, some years later, among the most useful mathematics that we have today, giving us data security and communications technology. Or look at the work on algebraic logic by George Boole some 150+ years ago. At the time, not even Boole thought it of any practical use but Boolean logic is now the foundation of modern computing. Speaking of computers, there were [non-Turing] mechanical computers invented thousands of years ago, along with electricity, steam power and other “modern” technology. However, these were seen as useless too, interesting curiosities only. My point here is that we can nearly never know whether some area of mathematics or other discipline might later become useful, or whether areas that are presently useful might later become useless. There is even a rule of thumb that says that only 5% of research will become useful within human time frames - but we unfortunately don’t know where those 5% lie. I am skeptical of the number “5%” because, as I’ve described, areas can fluctuate in importance. However, it could be worth conducting research into more certain ways of locating those “5%” of useful research. Perspective III: What maths to study? If you are thinking of completing a maths-related degree and are wondering about what to study in order to get a job, then I recommend studying a solid component of pure maths in order to train your brain, and add some coding and statistics in order to broaden your skill set. That will give you a solid foundation of depth and versatility, and will allow you to be able to take on a very wide range of jobs. In some countries, industrial culture would still prefer that you are trained narrowly, so as to step into a job after studies without need for much any job training. However, this is not a good longterm investment, especially since the nature of jobs is generally becoming both global and fluid, breaking old patterns and requiring independent thinking and adaptability. Jobs are becoming increasingly mathematical too, so solid training in independent mathematical thinking and ability is increasingly important. As for which areas of pure maths to study, I recommend mostly choosing what you like and are good at, as far as this is possible within the framework of your degree and overall direction.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Why do some people consider mathematics to be the most beautiful subject in academics?
Answer: We find many things beautiful, like the face of someone we love, or some favourite food or music or a good book, and there are many different flavours of beauty here. The underlying reasons for us to see beauty in things, however, are that our brains give us drugs that make us happy to experience beauty, and the sense of beauty is in turn enhanced through that happy and addictive reward. The sense of beauty in mathematics is neurologically very similar, it turns out, to the sense of beauty in art, music, a pretty face, fairness, or an interesting story, say. There seem to be two components of this sense of beauty. One is that our brains reward us with dopamine happiness when we successfully find patterns and explanations and solve problems, and there is plenty of opportunity to do that with all the symmetries, patterns, puzzles and discoveries of mathematics. If we call this component “order”, then the other component could be called “chaos”. Mathematics is full of surprising and unexpected discovery, and our brains also give us happy drug rewards when we encounter the unexpected; this is our sense of humour, and conducting mathematics can actually be quite exciting, fun and even funny. So, for many mathematicians and others, maths is beautiful because our brains reward us for solving problems, recognising patterns, discovering the new and unexpected. For some, these rewards can even be addictive, and I have met several people who have felt something like being in love with the practice of doing maths. These days, science is a huge field and has given us lots of answers. We can find beauty in lots of areas of science but many still find maths to be the richest source of raw and undiluted problems to solve, patterns to recognise, and exciting new things to discover, uncluttered by distracting and messy reality. Historical inertia has also played a part in the view of maths as beautiful. Thousands of years ago, science was young and often far less fertile in answers, so mathematics might have been seen as a relatively richer and more reliable source of discernible answers, recognisable patterns and new and exciting discoveries. In those days, mathematics often overlapped with other sources of beauty, such as philosophy, music, art, ethics, and mysticism, and in each of these disciplines, people not only enjoyed the sense of beauty but also associated these disciplines with beauty, sometimes even divine beauty. Mathematics was worshiped as being divine and most beautiful by Plato and his followers, and strong traditions like these can get propagated through history, especially when they are given regular boosts of adulation by new and addicted devotees. This worship can create mythology, and maths is rich with tales of heroic [and genius, or admirably eccentric] mathematicians, and dogma on how maths is “eternal” or “true” or “pure” or “the language of the universe”, and so on. This mythology is enjoyed by many devotees of maths, or rather, the idea of maths, and it has sometimes enhanced their perception of beauty in maths. So, to answer briefly: mathematics is seen as particularly beautiful because our brains make us happy when [successfully] doing mathematics and because there has been a long history and tradition of seeing maths as such. Personally, I love parts of mathematics [particularly combinatorics] and find these parts beautiful, exciting and satisfying to work, play and explore in: I am a happy addict :) PS: Here’s a (nervous and slightly fumbled) TEDx talk that I gave about this topic, with a couple more details. At some point, I’d like to write up a far more comprehensive survey of the mathematical aspects of the sense of beauty and all our other emotions.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: What is the goal of mathematics research? What do we gain from advances in the field of math?
Answer: There are many possible answers, depending on history and culture and outlook. Today, many people would answer that modern science and technology relies on maths, and in order to get better science and technology, we need better maths. Most mathematicians would probably answer that gaining mathematical knowledge is an aim in itself, just like most people these days see an inherent value in growing our scientific knowledge. Many of these mathematicians [including myself] would also add that it is challenging and exciting to conduct mathematical research, and that we gain pleasure, excitement, and contentment from doing this. In this way, you can view maths as a sport, as a hobby, as adventure and exploration, or even as meditation. Some also see mathematics as an art form. Indeed, it lights up the same parts of the brain for appreciating beauty as music and visual art, for instance, at least for those who have enough training to be able appreciate maths. Mathematical research can therefore be seen as the production of art, and just like other beautiful art, it is its own goal. There are other answers too. Looking into the past, maths was for large parts of history intimately part of cosmology and religion and mysticism. Finding new maths was to discover sacred knowledge, and this was treasured and protected jealously like other sacred knowledge. Looking into the future, our views on maths and on its use and value will presumably change again, perhaps once AI takes over the menial tasks of us mathematicians today. Maths might even lose its central, if to most people under-appreciated, role in our lives, once our technology and understanding of the world advances beyond what the window of maths can show us.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: What is a Millennium Prize problem?
Answer: The Millennium Prize problems are seven famous mathematical problems that have been highlighted to the general public in 2000 by the Clay Mathematics Institute, a non-profit foundation whose aim is to promote and disseminate mathematical knowledge. To make the mostly technical and arcane problems interesting to the public, the Institute is offering the prize of $1,000,000 for the solution of any of these. One of the problems has been solved, by Grigori Perelman who famously refused both the Millennium Prize and other prestigious prizes including the Fields Medal and the prize of the European Mathematical Society, offered to him for this and earlier mathematical achievements. Perelman’s refusal of the Millennium Prize was a snub to the Clay Mathematics Institute and their Millennium Prize concept but also made these problems all the more famous and newsworthy. Each of the problems are arguably more valuable as icons than for the potential knowledge that solving them would bring. Iconic problems can be useful for motivating researchers to work hard and deep towards the solution of such problems, and thereby create much valuable incidental knowledge. For instance, the Four Colour Problem was e eventually solved but was never given a satisfying solution and yet, for a century and a half, it provided motivation for researchers to develop a range of mathematics, even after its solution, that together with other research led to the development of computer science. The iconic status of the problems can also be used for publicity purposes, to attract more students to study and pursue mathematics as a career, and to persuade funding agencies to provide more support for mathematical research and education. The Millennium Prize problem may be seen as an updated continuation of the public highlighting of important unsolved mathematical problems by the eminent mathematician David Hilbert in 1900. Hilbert’s 23 problems gave rise to significant international attention and mathematical effort, and have been widely influential on the development of mathematics during the 20th century and even today. Some of the 23 problems have been solved; others remain unsolved. One is replicated as a Millennium Prize problem, the Riemann Hypothesis.

Name: Thomas Britz
Question: Is everything ultimately mathematical?
Answer: No; in fact, very little has a mathematical explanation. If you wake up and feel happy, then you would presumably not reach out for a pen and paper to mathematically work out why you were happy. In other words, maths is not very useful for explaining most things in our experience; nor is physics, chemistry or even biology for that matter. Shifting your focus away from your personal experience, mathematics becomes more useful. For instance, if we look at more than just ourselves, at a group of people, or if we look at our general behaviour, not just isolated experiences and actions, then patterns emerge that we can describe mathematically and statistically, sometimes even very simply - we are very often simple and predictable creatures. The explanations that maths gives us here are fuzzy though: uncertain averages and probabilities. Instead of looking at broader pictures, we could also look closer at things and, there, maths again begins to give useful explanations. Biology, chemistry, physics: as we look closer and closer at the small details of things, they begin to behave in very mathematically explainable ways. How useful those explanations might be is debatable though: they are good enough for us to use for creating the technology that we have today but it is still very clunky: our computer chips are literally stone age creations, silicon rock etched into tools. Mother Nature kicks our ass when it comes to tech. And when we look very closely at things, at quantum level, then uncertainty suddenly rears up again, and we can only describe a scattering of general patterns that we think that we have found and therefore call “Laws” but do not have any great predictive power; indeed, as far as we know, our putative reality is intrinsically unknowable, and certainly not mathematically deterministic. We can talk about probabilities but those do not generally provide any great sort of explanation. At a more philosophical level, we don’t know whether our realities and experiences have anything to do with mathematics, or whether mathematics is just one mental framework through which we see the world. There is sometimes fierce debate about this question. Many science-loving people point out that maths has let us perform many magics via science and technology and that maths has not yet let us down through contradictions or erratic predictive powers; therefore, maths must be universally true, everywhere and everywhen - indeed the world might be built from maths itself. Others disagree and point out the logical error here: it is too excitedly optimistic to claim that all of existence is maths-related just because we seem to have had success in understanding a tiny speck of the world through maths. That said, maths is nevertheless surprisingly useful for describing the world, ourselves and even our everyday experiences. Most people would not imagine it but if you have a little interest or training in mathematical thinking, then you can suddenly see a lot of patterns and explanations in everything around you that can allow you to see clearer and further. Maths is definitely very useful for explaining many things, just not great for explaining most things.

Most people would not imagine it but if you have a little interest or training in mathematical thinking, then you can suddenly see a lot of patterns and explanations in everything around you that can allow you to see clearer and further. Maths is definitely very useful for explaining many things, just not great for explaining most things.

Question: Could aliens arrive at our planet one day with a superior technology and prove that everything we know about maths and physics is wrong?
Answer: Sure; in fact, famous “aliens” like Newton, Gauss, Cantor, Bohr, Einstein, Goedel and countless others have done this many times over. The one thing that we know with some certainty is that we know nothing with absolute certainty; in fact, the whole of our [semi]modern Science is built on that assumption: we pretend to believe what we have of results and theories right now - we could call this our local truth - but are ever searching for new ideas and evidence that can prove us wrong, so that we can gain more sophisticated “truths”. Meanwhile, alien technology is all around us but far too advanced for us to understand it: Nature and even our own bodies and minds. It’s not long ago that we discovered DNA - the hardware of life but more complicated - and it’s pretty much just this millenia that we discovered epigenetics - the software of life but much more complicated. Once-head of the Human Genome Project, Eric Lander, was entheusiastic about all the huge new advances in medicine and genetics that these new discoveries have brought but also foretold that we would not properly understand any of this technology for centuries to come. Imagine what discoveries lie in wait in such a massive treasure trove of alien technology! Big truths often emerge from little observations, like the experiments of Michelson and Morley, or even the musings of visionaries. Four centuries ago, John Dunne pointed out in a poem that we cannot build even just the smallest leaf, and we still can’t. Until we can, then there is much to learn, not only about leaf-making but about our world, reality and ourselves.

Question: What are the implications of complete solutions for each of the Clay Institute Millenium Problems?
Answer: Most big and iconic problems like “Curb climate change”, or “Eradicate malaria” or “End world poverty” seek solutions to specific ends. In contrast, the Clay Institute Millenium Problems and most other famous mathematical conjectures provide specific ends to solutions: these problems and conjectures primarily serve as motivating catalysers for researchers to look hard and deep and sideways in order to come up with new and excellent mathematical results and theory. So, while complete solutions to each problem would undoubtedly have merit and application, the problems are not that important in and of themselves. Indeed, one might celebrate the triumphant solutions of some big problem but such solution is also cause for mourning: the death of a centuries old problem makes that problem inert and useless as motivator for future research.

Question: How does cos pi equal to -1?
Answer: When we write cos(x), we could actually mean either of two standard trigonometric functions which are different from each other but which, confusingly, are written using the same symbols. The first function, cos(x), is the cosine function where x is in degrees, 360 degrees being the number of degree needed to complete a full rotation around a circle. Here, cos(0) = 1, cos(90) = 0, and cos(180) = -1 . The second function, cos(x), is the cosine function where x is in radians, 2 π being the number of radians needed to complete a full rotation around a circle. Here, cos(0) = 1, cos( π /2) = 0, and cos( π ) = -1 . As you might see, the two functions cos(x) are basically the same, except for the different scaling of the input variable x. It is a bit awkward and sometimes confusing to have two functions share the same name but it is worth it here, since it is often useful to deal with degrees, and, at other times, it is more useful to deal with radians. Loosely speaking, degrees are useful for angles and many practical uses, whereas radians are good for mathematical identities and proofs as well as for circle circumferences (the circumference of a circle with radius 1 is 2 π , or the distance going one full walk around such a circle) . There are also two standard types of functions for sin(x), tan(x) and other trigonometric functions. You sometimes need to look at the context in which these functions appear to figure out which type of function is being used: degree-based or radian-based.

Question: I have difficult solving problems at Brilliant.org, does that mean I don't understand math?

Question: Who invented the integration of mathematics?
Answer: Some of the earliest instances of mathematical integration were due to the ancient Greeks Eudoxus (around 370BC) and, a little later, Archimedes, and it has been argued that the Babylonians invented integration methods before the Greeks. Chinese mathematicians also invented integration: Liu Hui in the 3rd century AD, and Zu Chongzhi and Zu Geng two centuries later. Integration in a more general and modern sense first appeared in the 17th and 18th centuries, in Europe and, independently, in Japan, by a number of mathematicians.
